desktop_reading_v1.headline: Turn a fault into a fix people can understand
desktop_reading_v1.scene: A prototype catches every time it opens or closes. First, test how the parts fit to see where they rub. Then check two measurements and draw two possible changes so the team can see the difference.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare prototype building, fault verification, and technical drawing. Ask who can follow a design from the first trial build through changes to the drawings.
desktop_reading_v1.question: For the last prototype problem, what made you decide to change a dimension or redesign a joint?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Make a hinged joint from cardboard. Compare two positions and draw what changed.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want another test fit or another round of checks, start with roles that give you access to samples. If explaining the fix was the best part, compare technical communication roles.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Technical roles can involve building from plans or diagnosing faults, testing changes, and drawing revisions yourself. Check for prototype testing, fault analysis, and design drawings in the posting.

RIA.headline: Build what is on the drawing
RIA.scene: A part that looks right on paper might not turn once it is fitted. When a prototype starts rubbing, you can trace the problem to its dimensions or materials and put the revised design in the next set of drawings.
RIA.career_lens: For prototype roles, look for hands-on assembly, testing, and adjustments. Ask who investigated the fault and delivered revised assembly drawings the last time a prototype failed a test. See whether you would own that work or rebuild it to somebody else's instructions.
RIA.question: When a recently assembled prototype jammed, what did a newcomer inspect personally? Could they put their changes in the assembly drawings?
RIA.trial: Make a freestanding bracket from two pieces of cardboard. Test an unstable joint, adjust it, and test it again. Sketch what changed.
RIA.decision: If you want another round of adjustments, start with jobs where you can assemble and test prototypes yourself. If you would rather find out why it wobbled or draw a better version, look for testing or design duties respectively.
RIA.screen: Mark the jobs that explicitly include prototype assembly and testing. Find out who traces faults and owns drawing revisions. Follow up on broad descriptions such as “support R&D.”
RIA.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you would build prototypes and modify parts yourself, and how much time is set aside for trial builds.

RAI.headline: Shape the material and the design together
RAI.scene: After folding a few sheets by hand, you start to see what kind of paper can hold the shape you want for a lampshade. Once you have an outline, test a few samples under the same light and compare the brightness and shadows.
RAI.career_lens: Find out who chooses the materials and makes the first sample. Some prototyping jobs also decide how it looks and feels, while others build to an approved design. Ask how you would test the sample and who does the testing.
RAI.question: When the materials first arrive, can a newcomer decide the sample's shape and how to make it? Who tests it before the design is finalized?
RAI.trial: Make two differently shaped desktop card holders from cardstock. Use the same card to test their stability and choose one.
RAI.decision: If making the object appealed most, look for trial builds. If you most wanted to decide the form or compare performance, check how often you would do that work.
RAI.screen: Check whether prototype work starts with choosing and shaping materials or begins only after design approval. Ask whether you can change the form and what the finished sample must pass.
RAI.hero_job_tip: If building and shaping things both appeal to you, ask whether you can choose materials, decide on a shape, and test samples.

IRA.headline: Trace an unusual sound to its cause
IRA.scene: A machine makes an unexpected noise under load. You might want to follow it to the source. Check the wear marks, swap a part for comparison, and draw the contact surface most easily reassembled the wrong way.
IRA.career_lens: Fault analysis should produce an explanation others can check. Ask whether you can use the equipment to reproduce the fault yourself and prepare a diagram for the next shift or repair team.
IRA.question: Who reproduced the last intermittent problem? Could a newcomer vary the conditions or only organize the observations?
IRA.trial: Use a paper clip to simulate a hanger that keeps falling. Change one condition at a time, record two results, and draw the most likely cause.
IRA.decision: If you want to rule out another explanation, look for access to original records and samples. If you most want to draw the explanation, consider technical communication.
IRA.screen: Look for jobs that deliver a reproducible fault or a report explaining its cause. Check access to samples and whether you diagram the investigation.
IRA.hero_job_tip: Start with roles where you can diagnose and verify faults. Ask who sets the conditions for each test.

IAR.headline: Test an explanation with a working model
IAR.scene: Several dimensions on the same drawing could explain why the pieces won't fit. You may enjoy sketching two possible designs, building simple models, and finding out which reproduces the jam.
IAR.career_lens: For testing and product development jobs, ask who proposes hypotheses and chooses how to test them. Some jobs turn findings into drawings and test a prototype on the bench. Others hand over a technical conclusion.
IAR.question: If the last experiment overturned a design, could a newcomer redraw it and test a model? What would they still own after handing it to design?
IAR.trial: Sketch two explanations for why a paper box tips over and how to test each. Use cardstock to try the test most likely to tell them apart.
IAR.decision: If following evidence and revising your judgment appealed most, look for control over the test. If you want to build the revision, look for roles that go from sketch to prototype.
IAR.screen: In product validation postings, mark proposing hypotheses, drawing options, and building prototypes. Find out which a newcomer actually delivers.
IAR.hero_job_tip: Find out whether models are built to investigate problems or mainly to demonstrate findings in presentations.

ARI.headline: Design a shape that feels right in the hand
ARI.scene: You might be most interested in how to curve the handle and how the object will look. Holding a clay model tells you whether that clean bend digs into your hand. Try two curves before choosing what to change.
ARI.career_lens: Ask whether the role can decide the form, material, or appearance. Some product designers make samples and revise them after load or durability tests. When others make and test the sample, more of your day may go into presenting the design.
ARI.question: What changed on the last piece because of production limits? Would a newcomer decide how it looks or build from someone else's drawing?
ARI.trial: Draw two versions of a small desktop object. Fold one out of paper and test how it sits.
ARI.decision: If you want to decide the form and keep revising it around real constraints, look for design with prototyping. If testing what works is more appealing, check the time set aside for tests.
ARI.screen: Look for jobs that propose forms, materials, or structures. Find out who makes samples and whether designers see durability or user testing.
ARI.hero_job_tip: For product design roles, ask which decisions you would help make as a sketch turns into a sample.

AIR.headline: Put the idea behind a design to a physical test
AIR.scene: You want a display stand to look lighter. A narrow frame and an offset support create different effects. Compare what each version obscures and how stable it is. Test both on a small sample before settling on an approach.
AIR.career_lens: Ask about the first review of an exhibit or visual design. Can you set the direction, revise the work after observation or testing, and follow it through to see how it looks once installed?
AIR.question: When an early design was hard to see on site, could a newcomer observe, change it, and check the result, or only update the drawing from comments?
AIR.trial: Make two signs for the same shelf. Put them up at different viewing distances and note which is easier to recognize.
AIR.decision: If you want to try another visual arrangement, look for a role with control over presentation. If you want to see it installed, ask whether you are responsible for the result on site.
AIR.screen: Compare whether the role delivers a concept, visitor feedback, or an installed piece. Mark where you can decide how it will look.
AIR.hero_job_tip: Check how much say you would have in the design and whether you would help test what happens when people use it.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Solve an on-site problem so others can handle it too
desktop_reading_v1.scene: A colleague keeps running into the same equipment issue after handover. Watch them work, distinguish a fault in the machine from a missed step, then show them what to do.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare the time and responsibility involved in troubleshooting on site, reviewing causes, and coaching others.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When someone new last helped troubleshoot a fault, at what step could they work on their own?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Choose a safe everyday tool. Note a way it can be used incorrectly and make a one-page troubleshooting guide.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: Notice which part you want to keep doing: handling the problem on site, explaining why it happened, or helping someone learn to handle it.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Both maintenance and on-site training can involve people and equipment. Maintenance usually ends when the machine is running again. In training, the outcome is whether someone can operate the machine independently.

RIS.headline: Find the fault and get the equipment running again
RIS.scene: A machine is down. You might be most drawn to getting it running again. Once you have adjusted the part, you can check why it failed at only one setting and walk the colleague on duty through the checks after restarting.
RIS.career_lens: In jobs that combine hands-on work with troubleshooting, find out whether you personally verify that the machine is running again. Some jobs also ask you to talk operators through your reasoning so they know what to check first when it happens again.
RIS.question: After a temporary fix, does a newcomer retest the equipment and explain the checks to the next shift?
RIS.trial: Use a cardboard box to mock up a lid that doesn't close smoothly. Make one adjustment and ask someone to repeat it using brief instructions. Note which step still needs a demonstration.
RIS.decision: If you want to troubleshoot another fault yourself, prioritize hands-on field work. If you also want to investigate recurring faults and demonstrate the fix, look for roles that include both diagnosis and training.
RIS.screen: Look for hands-on checks and troubleshooting. Then ask whether you can investigate recurring faults and show new colleagues how to handle them.
RIS.hero_job_tip: Ask how a typical day divides between troubleshooting, replacing parts, and handover, and which faults you'd diagnose yourself.

RSI.headline: Set the equipment up for the person taking over
RSI.scene: You might want to stay by the workbench and adjust a machine that's hard to learn. Demonstrating it and watching a new colleague try it can show whether the equipment or the instructions are causing trouble.
RSI.career_lens: Assembly and training can both mean using tools. Find out whether you finish when equipment is set up or also demonstrate it, watch where new operators make mistakes, and check whether the procedure, equipment, or instructions caused the problem.
RSI.question: Who decides when a newcomer can work on their own? If they repeatedly miss one step, can this role change the demo or check the equipment settings?
RSI.trial: Choose a safe tabletop assembly step. Show it once and let someone try. Note whether the movement, tool, or instruction stops them.
RSI.decision: If you want hands-on operation with some teaching, look for on-site training. If spotting patterns in mistakes interests you more, compare training quality or fault diagnosis.
RSI.screen: Compare time operating equipment, demonstrating on shift, and recording the reasons for mistakes. Ask whether training ends at a demonstration or at independent operation.
RSI.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you hand over equipment after setup, teach others to operate it, or follow up when they run into a problem.

IRS.headline: Follow the clues on site to find where work gets stuck
IRS.scene: Why does the same batch fail only on the night shift? Compare machine logs and actual samples, then walk through the operation with someone who was on duty. Each check narrows what could have changed.
IRS.career_lens: Ask whether a technical investigation ends in a report or a procedure that has been checked on site and operators can follow. The second means handling actual equipment and listening to users' questions.
IRS.question: If a fault rarely happens, can a newcomer decide how to reproduce it? Will they also explain the result to the people on site?
IRS.trial: Think of two reasons a drawer might keep catching. Simulate it with a cardboard box at two angles, see whether the comparison separates the causes, and tell someone what to check first.
IRS.decision: If you want to investigate the remaining causes, look for time to retest. If showing others how to handle it matters more, look for a team that lets researchers work on site.
IRS.screen: Look for roles that devise ways to investigate problems. Check whether you retest them personally and explain the findings to operators.
IRS.hero_job_tip: Start with work that gives you access to original records and samples and lets you verify what happened with the people on site.

ISR.headline: Find out why people keep asking for the same help
ISR.scene: Several operators report trouble after changing materials. You might want to know whether they are describing the same fault. Compare the equipment when it's empty and when it's loaded, and use the result to help the people on shift.
ISR.career_lens: Look for access to interviews and actual operating records if you want to identify recurring issues from people's feedback. Ask whether you can return to the site and test a change with users after finding the cause.
ISR.question: When users say a step is too hard, can a newcomer watch them try and verify why? What happens to the findings afterward?
ISR.trial: Ask someone to follow public instructions for a simple tabletop task. Ask where they are unsure, observe what they do, and write one possible cause to check.
ISR.decision: If you want to find why people keep struggling, keep roles with first-hand evidence. For direct support or making changes, check whether the role includes testing on site.
ISR.screen: Look for investigations that use interviews and actual operating records. Find out whether you propose a fix or also test it where it is used.
ISR.hero_job_tip: Ask who confirms the cause once requests are grouped together, and whether you would see the equipment or test it on site.

SRI.headline: Work through a difficult step alongside a newcomer
SRI.scene: You might care most about the moment a newcomer can take over without your help. Clamp the workpiece together again, check whether the grip feels awkward or the fixture blocks their view, and decide what to practice next.
SRI.career_lens: On-site support may mean teaching someone to operate the equipment or fixing a fault for them. Ask how the last ticket was closed: when the person could work independently, or after someone investigated why the error kept occurring?
SRI.question: After helping a user resume work, does the newcomer investigate similar failures or hand them over to another team?
SRI.trial: Walk someone through a paper fold you know. Demonstrate as needed and record where they get stuck across two tries, with possible causes.
SRI.decision: If you want to keep helping people finish, prioritize direct support. If you liked handling the fault or tracing the cause more, compare repair and research work.
SRI.screen: Start with technical support that demonstrates tasks and answers questions live. Ask who handles the tools and who checks recurring faults.
SRI.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can demonstrate tasks yourself and change the setup when a new colleague gets stuck.

SIR.headline: Start teaching again at the point where someone got stuck
SIR.scene: Some people understand an instruction immediately. Others try it three times and get nowhere. You could ask what they think the next step is, then show what it means using the real part.
SIR.career_lens: In training evaluation or technical support, ask whether you hear directly where learners get stuck. Then find out whether you deliver an analysis or can redo the task on the equipment and check a revised demonstration.
SIR.question: The last time several people reported the same problem, did support staff help follow up and test it on the equipment?
SIR.trial: Ask someone to describe a real difficulty learning a task and when it occurred. Demonstrate a possible change with a paper model and ask whether it helps.
SIR.decision: If following the same person's progress appeals most, look for roles with follow-up. If you want to verify a common cause, look for time set aside to investigate.
SIR.screen: Ask whether you work regularly with the same users. Check whether you mainly answer questions or can investigate patterns and test changes yourself.
SIR.hero_job_tip: Look for roles where you can adapt coaching to each person's sticking point and demonstrate using the actual equipment.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Find support for a fix you've already tested
desktop_reading_v1.scene: An old production line keeps stopping during material changes. Reproduce the fault, identify whether it comes from the material or the procedure, and ask the people involved to approve a small trial.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare troubleshooting, engineering improvement, and project coordination. Identify the part this job owns.
desktop_reading_v1.question: After making a recommendation, can someone in this role secure resources for a trial, or do they submit an analysis for others to use?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Use paper pieces to model two layouts. Note how long each takes to use, then write a three-sentence proposal for a trial.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you also want to coordinate work after a trial, look for jobs responsible for putting improvements into practice.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: In technical support or solutions roles, ask whether you can reproduce a problem yourself. Check how much time goes into getting a pilot running and how much into closing sales.

RIE.headline: Troubleshoot a fault yourself before deciding what to do
RIE.scene: You might be drawn to testing equipment in person before it goes into use. If a workpiece keeps slipping during a test fit, compare ways of clamping it. Bring your measurements to the person responsible and discuss whether to make a new fixture.
RIE.career_lens: For repair or implementation work, first check whether you personally locate and fix faults. If the posting also mentions making improvements, ask whether you retest changes and whether you provide evidence or apply for downtime and resources yourself.
RIE.question: When the last fix required downtime, did a newcomer test it and request permission, or carry out an approved plan?
RIE.trial: Use cardboard to model a cover that's hard to remove. Try a joint that opens more easily, note what changed, and write two sentences on the fix and time needed.
RIE.decision: If you mostly want to improve the equipment, prioritize hands-on work. If you want to win support for the change, ask whether you can use the test results to secure resources.
RIE.screen: Find roles that locate and repair problems in person. Mark who retests afterward and who asks for downtime or an improvement budget.
RIE.hero_job_tip: Ask if the role includes on-site diagnosis and whether your findings can shape purchasing or repair decisions.

REI.headline: Bring a working prototype to the proposal meeting
REI.scene: You might most want to make a sample that works on site. Let the business team try it, find out which change it will fund, and run a comparison test to settle the remaining questions.
REI.career_lens: Pilot work can mean installing something according to a plan or arranging which teams try it and collecting the measurements. Ask who changes the plan on site when something goes wrong and who decides whether to extend the trial.
REI.question: If a pilot runs short of staff or materials, can the people on site change the plan? Who checks whether it worked?
REI.trial: Arrange a shared desk with someone. Test one layout yourself, agree on responsibilities, and count how often you reach for items before and after changing the layout.
REI.decision: If making it work yourself mattered most, favor implementation roles. If getting the arrangements in place was more appealing, check whether you have control over scheduling.
REI.screen: Mark duties that include both implementation and rescheduling. Ask whether you only leave equipment usable or also deliver a record of pilot tests.
REI.hero_job_tip: For technical project roles, check whether you would build prototypes yourself and how much time resource coordination takes.

IRE.headline: Investigate why repairs are coming back so the team can decide what to change
IRE.scene: Several batches of the same part have suddenly come back for repair. You might want to know when the trouble started. Compare wear marks across two batches and recreate the issue on a test bench before discussing replacement with a supervisor.
IRE.career_lens: Check whether the job gives you time to run a comparison test as well as prepare presentation material. You may need to show that a fix works with physical measurements and explain errors and limitations to get approval for a trial.
IRE.question: When results are uncertain, does the analyst explain them directly to decision-makers and ask for another test?
IRE.trial: Fold two paper bridges using different methods. Add the same small items in order, record what you see and what you can't determine, and request a follow-up test.
IRE.decision: If you want to rule out errors before deciding, look for time to test. If you want findings to shape a decision, look for research roles involved in pilot discussions.
IRE.screen: Look for work with comparison tests. Mark whether you handle the samples directly and prepare evidence for a pilot decision.
IRE.hero_job_tip: Look for roles where you can set up your own test and make the case to decision-makers once you understand the cause.

IER.headline: Use what you found to make the case for a change
IER.scene: You might want to know whether late deliveries stem from equipment or the way work is organized. Bring data and two options to a discussion. If the team gives you time for a pilot, go on site to see whether the change cuts waiting time.
IER.career_lens: In technical solutions roles, distinguish analyzing which option works from taking an approved solution to the site. Find out whether the job also coordinates installation windows and verifies results on site once you have the evidence.
IER.question: After submitting the analysis, can a newcomer discuss trial conditions with the people implementing it and check the results on site?
IER.trial: Compare how people reach items stored in two places. Summarize the evidence, get someone to try moving the items once, and check what changes.
IER.decision: If you mainly want to find out which option works, keep roles with authority to investigate. If you want to implement the change, check that you can reach the person responsible.
IER.screen: Check whether the job begins by investigating or receives a plan already chosen. Mark who negotiates resources and who goes on site to check the result.
IER.hero_job_tip: Ask who needs to be persuaded by the findings and who runs the pilot or implements it on site.

ERI.headline: Turn an equipment improvement into an on-site pilot
ERI.scene: You might be drawn to getting everyone to free up a production line for a trial. Use a working sample to agree on the scope and decide in advance which measurements would justify expanding the pilot.
ERI.career_lens: If you want to start pilots, ask who decides which resources and people to involve. Then find out whether you can adjust the installation on site and whether the pilot ends with a status report or a new decision based on retesting.
ERI.question: Who chose the people for the last pilot, adjusted things on site, and decided whether to continue?
ERI.trial: Ask someone to try a new spot for a shared item. Agree on the location and who puts it back. After a day, check whether it's easier to get.
ERI.decision: If you enjoyed bringing people together and deciding the setup, look for coordination duties. If you also want to verify the result, make sure the role can get on site.
ERI.screen: Find roles that can start projects and organize resources. Ask who helps set up a pilot and who reviews the result.
ERI.hero_job_tip: Compare jobs where you can negotiate for resources and still join the on-site pilot. Find out who can make the decision.

EIR.headline: Use the data to negotiate a change the site can carry out
EIR.scene: You might be most interested in getting people to agree to an upgrade. Compare the cost of downtime with the cost of each fix. If the team needs a demonstration, make a small physical modification to show what would work.
EIR.career_lens: Technical sales might deliver orders or approved implementation plans. Ask whether you verify evidence on the customer's site and whether you still have a role in installation or retesting once the agreement is signed.
EIR.question: If a customer challenges the proposal, can someone in this role check the site and revise the commitment?
EIR.trial: Write trial conditions for a mock equipment layout. Ask someone to raise an objection, then check one concern using a paper layout or simple measurement.
EIR.decision: If securing an agreement appealed more than testing, look for roles that move proposals forward. If evidence interested you most, check who actually does the investigation.
EIR.screen: For technical solutions roles, ask whether success means a sale, a pilot, or a feasibility finding. Check whether you would see the place or samples yourself.
EIR.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the role is mainly evaluated on securing decisions, producing analysis, or carrying out the work.

strategy_label: Hands-on, inquiry, and process: three clues to observe
activity_chain: Observe through three separate activity entry points: work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions; analyze questions, evidence, variables, or ways of explaining; organize rules, data, processes, order, or reviewable records.
core_reading: These three leading interest dimensions indicate that Realistic, Investigative, and Conventional activities stand relatively high in this response. They can help organize exploration and questions, but cannot establish a personality identity, ability level, or career conclusion.
positive_value: The value of this content is to break the clues into observable small tasks: Realistic focuses on tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results; Investigative focuses on questions, evidence, mechanisms, variables, and ways of explaining; Conventional focuses on rules, data, processes, order, and reviewable records. Whichever comes first only indicates which activity to gather evidence from first. These clues offer exploration questions, not job answers.
real_world_cost: Reading boundary: these three clues may occur in different parts of one task or across different environments. Record only the appeal of specific activities, points of hesitation, and conditions you want to adjust. Do not turn the score order into a ranking of abilities or a fixed way of working.
first_experiment: Spend 30 minutes on a low-risk observation: in the first 10 minutes, bring materials, equipment, samples, or on-site constraints into view; in the next 10 minutes, pose a question and check evidence and relationships between variables; in the final 10 minutes, clearly organize the steps, fields, rules, or records of checks. Record only which action you most want to continue.
low_risk_validation: Low-risk observation: choose a small task that accommodates hands-on, inquiry, and process clues. Record the three activities separately and look only at activity preferences and evidence of wanting to continue.
primary_activity_chain: Start with the first dimension, Realistic: use it as the initial observation entry point and look for small-task evidence involving tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results.
secondary_support_line: Then consider the second dimension, Investigative: use it as an additional observation entry point and record whether questions, evidence, mechanisms, variables, and ways of explaining make the task more appealing.
tertiary_stabilizer: The third dimension, Conventional, is only an additional clue: observe whether rules, data, processes, order, and reviewable records help distinguish more specific task conditions.
activity_sequence: Initial observation entry point: work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions
Second observation entry point: analyze questions, evidence, variables, or ways of explaining
Third observation entry point: organize rules, data, processes, order, or reviewable records
free_page_teaser: Realistic, Investigative, and Conventional interest clues can be observed in sequence without rushing to a career answer.
ordered_code_handling: The ordered three-letter code describes the reading order for this assessment: the first letter is the initial observation entry point, and the second and third are additional entry points. The order changes what to ask first and what to validate next. It is not a fixed identity, an ability conclusion, or a career answer.
likely_tension: Differences between the three clues are worth exploring through small tasks. Observing one action and one condition at a time is more reliable than treating the three leading interests as a fixed way of working.
when_to_use_140q: When a user wants to distinguish whether task activities, environmental conditions, or role responsibilities are more appealing, 140Q can be an option. 140Q only adds contextual detail; it does not increase accuracy or override 60Q.
when_not_to_overread: When response quality is low, the leading scores are close, content is missing, or the user only wants to see the names, return to observing activities rather than offering strong interpretations.
deep_report_extension: Further reading can distinguish preference evidence across tasks, environments, and role responsibilities, and offer exploration questions and follow-up actions.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Turn one repair into a procedure for next time
desktop_reading_v1.scene: The machine is running again. Find out why it failed, what confirms the repair, and where the next shift should look if it happens again.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare field maintenance, quality investigation, and process maintenance by what each delivers: a repair, evidence, or a traceable record.
desktop_reading_v1.question: The second time the same fault happens, who gets to change the inspection procedure?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Simulate a missed inspection. Write a possible cause, a way to check it, and a handover note.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you most want to prevent the same fault from recurring, look for quality or process improvement jobs with access to the site.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Equipment maintenance and quality inspection both encounter faults. Maintenance commonly restores equipment to working order. Inspection more often checks the records and leaves results others can verify.

RIC.headline: Find out why the repair hasn't held
RIC.scene: When a part repeatedly refuses to fit, finding where it catches may be the part that interests you. Compare wear on two pieces, try a replacement, then add the relevant measurement to the maintenance checklist.
RIC.career_lens: In maintenance roles, ask whether you personally get equipment running again. Quality or reliability jobs can also involve handling equipment, often to retest results and rule out chance. The record then shows where the failure came from and how far the fix has gone.
RIC.question: After equipment is working again, does a newcomer confirm it runs or have to reproduce the original fault and record the result?
RIC.trial: Make a paper lid that opens and closes. Fix where it catches, repeat the motion three times, and record when it still catches.
RIC.decision: If working with your hands appealed most, look for direct repair. If you also want to retest and document the result, find field roles with quality responsibility.
RIC.screen: Mark hands-on troubleshooting, repeat tests, and acceptance records. Note which task keeps coming up in an ordinary week.
RIC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can troubleshoot maintenance problems directly and what standard you use to hand over findings.

RCI.headline: Get each assembled machine through its acceptance checks
RCI.scene: You might want to assemble equipment so it runs reliably. Check torque, clearances, and the first run against acceptance criteria. When something is out of range, take a unit aside to find out why.
RCI.career_lens: When a posting says you will work to specifications, check whether you make finished goods or inspect them each day. When measurements are out of tolerance, find out whether you can remeasure and check the fixtures and materials, or whether the main duty is reporting and returning the rejected part.
RCI.question: When the last batch was out of tolerance, could a newcomer check materials and tools, or only record and return the parts?
RCI.trial: Fold three paper pieces to the same dimensions, record deviations, and check whether the biggest one came from measuring, folding, or cutting.
RCI.decision: If you want to make things regularly and check them against standards, look for production with inspection. If the cause is most interesting, ask whether you can investigate the process.
RCI.screen: Compare making and inspecting parts. Check whether you handle them every day, what specifications apply, and how far you can investigate an exception.
RCI.hero_job_tip: In assembly roles, compare time spent on the equipment and checking records. Find out who investigates faults.

IRC.headline: Use a sample to find out what's causing the anomaly
IRC.scene: A few parts in one batch are wearing out early. You may want to find what they have in common. Reproduce the operating load with a sample and use the batch number to find the production record and rule out possible causes.
IRC.career_lens: Ask what a process validation role delivers: reproducible test results or a checklist of items that passed. Find out whether you can design actual tests and add the validated conditions to inspection procedures.
IRC.question: When two runs of the same method disagree, can a newcomer design a retest? Can the revised method go into the inspection procedure?
IRC.trial: Define one load test for a paper bridge, compare two structures, record where each fails, and turn reproducible checks into checklist items.
IRC.decision: If you want to design another comparison, start with validation work. If you prefer doing tests or maintaining standards, check how much time those tasks take.
IRC.screen: Look for roles that choose how to test a result. Ask whether you do the test and whether you deliver findings alone or revise the inspection checklist too.
IRC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can work with samples and a test bench or mainly draw conclusions from summary records.

ICR.headline: Find an anomaly in the records worth testing
ICR.scene: You might notice that scrap counts unexpectedly rose on a few days. Match batch numbers to machine records and choose a few parts to inspect. That lets you check whether the problem is actually concentrated in one place.
ICR.career_lens: In quality analysis, finding out that readings are drifting is a starting point. Ask whether you can update measurement definitions and retest a sample when results are disputed, or whether you pass the error record on to a lab or field team.
ICR.question: When the records and physical items disagree, who can retrieve originals, ask for another inspection, and change how the table records the results?
ICR.trial: Make a fictional equipment list with one inaccurate quantity. Compare it with small objects in a box and write where the error might have started.
ICR.decision: If you want to trace the source, look for original data and field feedback. If keeping records consistent matters more, look at maintaining standards.
ICR.screen: In data quality or reliability, mark tasks that investigate unusual figures. Ask whether you can change recording rules or send each anomaly to the field team.
ICR.hero_job_tip: Check whether you can set your own questions and follow an anomaly from the data back to the site.

CRI.headline: Build physical inspection into a process that others can verify
CRI.scene: Miss one check and the next shift might keep using an incorrect reading. This is the kind of handover you may want to make more reliable. Follow an operator through an inspection, compare measurements where readings repeatedly differ, and record exactly where to take the measurement.
CRI.career_lens: Some inspectors check each item against a common standard. Others also investigate which process introduced a deviation. Ask whether you can recheck samples and start an investigation as well as sign off on the record.
CRI.question: When the same check repeatedly fails, does a newcomer document evidence, retest it, or pass the problem to engineering?
CRI.trial: Set three appearance checks for similar cardboard boxes. Inspect and record each one. Investigate one case where the results disagree.
CRI.decision: If you want to check quality and leave traceable records, look for inspection responsibilities. If you prefer changing the item or investigating, see whether rework or research is part of the job.
CRI.screen: Mark tasks that verify items to the specification. Ask whether you handle samples and whether you investigate causes when something fails.
CRI.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can set inspection standards and check items on site, or mainly review results other people have filed.

CIR.headline: Leave a record so the next person can investigate the anomaly
CIR.scene: You might want to put scattered maintenance records in an order others can verify. Trace one questionable reading through equipment logs and batch records. If necessary, ask for another measurement and leave enough information to trace it.
CIR.career_lens: In quality work that keeps records traceable, ask what happens once a discrepancy is found. You might review previous batches and recommend retesting a sample or simply log the outcome according to procedure.
CIR.question: When the standard last disagreed with what happened on site, could the person maintaining it see the original material and request a new check?
CIR.trial: Use a fictional parts list to build a one-page acceptance record. Find one discrepancy and check it against a physical object.
CIR.decision: If you like keeping records traceable and can see yourself repeating the checks, start with quality or documentation roles. If finding causes matters more, check who can investigate.
CIR.screen: Compare process maintenance with reviewing exceptions. Check whether both primary data and results from physical retests are available.
CIR.hero_job_tip: For quality or process jobs, ask how often you fill in forms, check for gaps, or investigate issues and change the recording rules.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make something someone else can learn to use
desktop_reading_v1.scene: An interactive exhibit is built, but visitors don't know where to press. Change the physical buttons or the instructions and see whether a newcomer can use it on their own.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Check whether the job involves prototype building, experience design, and people using the item on site.
desktop_reading_v1.question: Once a sample is made, who watches how people use it and who can revise the next version?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Make a paper mock-up of a button interface. Let someone try it and change a prompt where they got stuck.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If altering the sample yourself was the most interesting part, confirm that the job owns some of the hands-on work.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: In exhibit, teaching aid, or interactive product roles, look for contact with physical objects and actual users. Some roles hand off a drawing. Others follow the work through to an on-site trial.

RAS.headline: Build something people can use to practice
RAS.scene: A good teaching tool comes apart and goes together in your hands, while showing a beginner where every part fits. You might enjoy building one, marking the tricky pieces, and letting someone see whether they can use it independently.
RAS.career_lens: In model, prop, or teaching aid jobs, first check whether you build a physical object from materials. Ask whether you can revise the design while building it and whether people get to try the sample. The answers show whether you would mainly build or also contribute to design and testing.
RAS.question: After the first sample, would a newcomer try it with users and make changes based on what they see?
RAS.trial: Make a movable sign out of cardstock, change its outline, and ask someone to use it to find a particular item. Record what wasn't obvious.
RAS.decision: If you want to build another sample, keep looking at production roles. If you want to change the shape or help people use it, check whether the job covers those parts.
RAS.screen: Look for making teaching tools or models by hand. Ask whether you can change the design during trial builds and let users try the finished piece.
RAS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you would build on site, how much room you have to change the design, and whether you can see people using it.

RSA.headline: Use the object in your hands to teach the movement
RSA.scene: You might enjoy a task you can try right away at the bench. Do it once yourself, let a newcomer practice, and use a color or sketch to mark the step that's easy to assemble backward.
RSA.career_lens: Compare the time you spend setting up exhibits and helping at live activities. If visitor traffic stalls, do you guide people and change the signs yourself, or report the issue to another team?
RSA.question: If visitors go the wrong way after an event starts, can a newcomer change the layout and signs? Who explains the change to visitors?
RSA.trial: Set up two zones for a tabletop activity. Walk someone through both and add a sign to answer the question they actually had.
RSA.decision: If you want to arrange the space again, prioritize on-site work. If you most want to greet people or design the signs, check how much time goes to each.
RSA.screen: Mark jobs where you actually set things up, then check whether you guide people on site and update the signs.
RSA.hero_job_tip: Check how much of the work involves handling objects and whether you can demonstrate and improve the teaching tools.

ARS.headline: Turn an idea into a piece people can experience
ARS.scene: An exhibition can begin with a display board or with a model visitors can turn. You might want to choose what people encounter first. Those alternatives draw attention to different things. Once the model is built to scale, you can try it with visitors.
ARS.career_lens: Follow a piece from concept to finished object. Who chooses the form and material, who builds it, and who watches how people use it? If you can participate in all three, find out whether you finish at delivery or revise it after people try it.
ARS.question: If a sample looks good and is hard to use, can a newcomer choose how to revise it and help build the next one?
ARS.trial: Sketch two paper sleeves that can be lifted with one hand. Build one, ask someone to pick it up, and mark what you would change.
ARS.decision: If you want to try another form, look for design authority. If you'd rather improve how it is made or used, find chances to follow the sample into user testing.
ARS.screen: Mark jobs where you decide the form of the final piece. Ask whether you can make a sample and observe someone using it.
ARS.hero_job_tip: In exhibition or experience design, find out who chooses the setting, builds the sample, and explains it to participants.

ASR.headline: Find a new way to explain a confusing experience
ASR.scene: You might be drawn to making an explanation work for the people taking part. Turn the instructions into a leaflet with one image per step, listen for confusion during practice, and update the leaflet and physical labels on the spot.
ASR.career_lens: When an experience design role mentions creativity, ask whether you decide where participants start and how they interact. Find out whether you can lead a trial run and use the feedback to change displays, props, or visitor routes.
ASR.question: When someone misses an interactive element, can a newcomer explain it again, adjust the prop, or change how the experience is arranged?
ASR.trial: Design a three-minute tabletop activity. Take someone through it and adjust one prop they didn't notice.
ASR.decision: If rearranging the experience interests you most, look for control over content. If you would rather guide people or make props, check typical time in those tasks.
ASR.screen: Look for work where you design what participants do first and how to explain it. Ask if you will guide visitors and adjust props.
ASR.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you can design the materials and coach participants, and who makes the tools they use.

SRA.headline: Help someone go from understanding a task to doing it
SRA.scene: Seeing someone make their first piece might make you want to keep teaching. Practice with materials beside them, resize a part that's awkward to hold, and color-code the sides that are easy to mix up.
SRA.career_lens: In practical training, learner independence can be one measure of success. Ask who demonstrates on the equipment, whether you practice with learners after mistakes, and whether you would revise the illustrations yourself.
SRA.question: If the last learner couldn't operate independently, did the newcomer keep practicing with them, demonstrate again, or revise the illustration?
SRA.trial: Guide someone through assembling a paper item and let them try independently. Draw a reminder for whichever part is easiest to reverse.
SRA.decision: If you want to keep practicing with people, look at direct teaching. Check whether you can demonstrate with objects and update the materials too.
SRA.screen: Look for jobs that coach people through an exercise and check whether they can do it alone. Ask whether demonstrations and producing materials belong to the same role.
SRA.hero_job_tip: In activity facilitation, ask how often you coach people directly, prepare materials, or adapt the tools yourself.

SAR.headline: Turn a hard-to-explain instruction into a demonstration
SAR.scene: When someone can't follow “clip it to the side,” you might be willing to keep trying ways to explain until they can do it alone. Their response can tell you whether a sketch, a gesture, or a demonstration sample works best.
SAR.career_lens: Some support roles make diagrams or models to explain a task. Others answer questions on site using existing materials. Ask whether you meet users directly and whether you can make a sample for them to try.
SAR.question: When someone says the instructions make sense but still can't do it, can you make an example they can try?
SAR.trial: Ask someone which step is hardest to follow. Draw it and make a paper example they can handle.
SAR.decision: If you want to follow up on whether someone can now do it, explore direct support. If you prefer drawing or making, ask whether you can own that part.
SAR.screen: Compare direct support with behind-the-scenes production. Look for jobs that let you understand a person's difficulty and revise the materials yourself.
SAR.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can meet learners and change the explanation, and how the job divides between making materials and showing the task in person.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make the sample and get a chance to try it
desktop_reading_v1.scene: A product could have two shapes. Make two rough versions people can hold, decide how to show the difference, and ask the team to try selling one of them.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare sample building, visual presentation, and delivering proposals. Some roles own only one.
desktop_reading_v1.question: On the last proposal, did the person who made the sample also present it and help decide what to keep?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Make two paper prototypes for the same small object. Outline how each would be used and one reason to test it.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want to iterate on samples and spend less of the week securing resources, prioritize roles with more production or design time.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Making a sample, preparing a presentation, and introducing a product are separate tasks. Ask what you actually get to make and whether convincing customers is a central measure of the job.

RAE.headline: Build a prototype that captures the idea
RAE.scene: Between a sketch and a working sample, you may most enjoy trying out materials, dimensions, and assembly methods. Once the sample works, refine its form and material and bring it, along with the cost trade-offs, to ask for another round of prototypes.
RAE.career_lens: Compare the time spent building a sample, changing its shape, and explaining it to others. Ask whether your responsibility ends with the sample or continues until a customer agrees to use it.
RAE.question: After a newcomer makes a sample, do they change how it is presented, demonstrate it, and find out whether it is adopted?
RAE.trial: Make a paper sample and change its appearance. Prepare a 30-second demonstration and ask someone if they would try it and why.
RAE.decision: If you want to keep making samples, prioritize prototype production. If seeing it adopted matters most, ask whether demonstrations and partner discussions are secondary tasks or measures of success.
RAE.screen: Use the stated deliverables to tell whether the work mainly builds samples, revises appearance, or presents the product and wins orders.
RAE.hero_job_tip: For sample development roles, ask how much you build yourself and how much time you spend pitching a design or securing a budget.

REA.headline: Use a physical sample to deliver on an improvement proposal
REA.scene: You might want to change a device that feels awkward to use. Show the revised part to the person responsible, explain the time and materials it needs, and use a label or detail in the shape to make the new use clear.
REA.career_lens: Some changes can be made by the person building the item. Others need permission from a venue or organizer. Ask who made the last decision and whether you can still change how the finished item is presented.
REA.question: If the space gets smaller at short notice, can a newcomer try another setup, negotiate a time to make changes, and rearrange it?
REA.trial: Use two sheets of paper to represent two sites. Set up a display and ask someone playing the venue owner to give you a restriction. Make a second version that works within it.
REA.decision: To keep solving physical space problems, look for installation duties. If negotiating the conditions was more appealing, also compare field coordination.
REA.screen: Find jobs that build on site and handle changes. Check whether you negotiate with the venue and revise the displays yourself.
REA.hero_job_tip: Look for roles where you can deliver an improvement and help it get adopted. Ask whether you decide how to present it.

ARE.headline: Show what you want to make with a sample
ARE.scene: You might be most interested in giving the product its form and feel. Putting a sample on site reveals what fits. Then you can show the person responsible how the versions differ and discuss which to keep.
ARE.career_lens: In product styling or installation design, ask which aspects of the appearance and experience you decide. Find out whether you make a sample yourself, explain the trade-offs in a review, and request time for another build.
ARE.question: At the last creative review, could a newcomer bring their own sample and explain the trade-offs? Who took over the revisions after feedback?
ARE.trial: Sketch two shapes for a display object, make one out of paper, and use it to explain your decision and ask for a trial installation.
ARE.decision: If you want to keep designing and building, look for creative decision-making. If the presentation and approval interested you more, check how success is assessed.
ARE.screen: Look for roles that can choose the form, make a sample, and present it for approval.
ARE.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you would take a design from concept to sample and whether you contribute to the proposal or own getting it approved.

AER.headline: Secure a chance to test a distinctive idea
AER.scene: You might enjoy coming up with a stand that stands out. Once the idea is clear, ask the organizers for space and budget. Use a small model to show what the structure and installation will require.
AER.career_lens: Some creative proposals go only as far as approval. Others require a budget, materials, and on-site setup. Ask whether you can change the physical result and whether the job is judged by the proposal, the event, or a commercial outcome.
AER.question: Once a proposal is approved, does a newcomer stay involved through installation? What can they change when the budget is tight?
AER.trial: Design a small exhibit and sketch what people see first. Agree on budget limits, then mock it up using what you have.
AER.decision: If developing the idea appealed most, keep roles with time for creative work. If you want it funded and built, check how the team splits those duties.
AER.screen: Mark which presentation decisions you would lead. Find out whether you also seek budget approval or set up the work on site.
AER.hero_job_tip: Ask what creative decisions you can make and how your time splits between pitching an idea and building it.

ERA.headline: Turn an agreement into something visible on site
ERA.scene: You might enjoy turning a customer's vague request into something both sides can agree to deliver. Use a working prototype to set the scope and ask a designer to show two versions of a detail so the customer can see what they are choosing.
ERA.career_lens: An event lead might set deadlines, coordinate suppliers, and oversee installation, or mainly get approval. Ask whether you handle constraints in person and who decides changes to visitor routes or displays.
ERA.question: The last time a display changed at short notice, who reassigned tasks and who could change the size or display order on site?
ERA.trial: Simulate a smaller venue. Reassign tasks between two people, shrink the layout, and draw a route visitors can still follow.
ERA.decision: If you wanted to get everyone working to the new plan, explore delivery coordination. If building or the look of the outcome mattered most, check dedicated roles in those areas.
ERA.screen: Find project roles that schedule the venue, staff, and work. Ask whether they also help install the display and revise its design.
ERA.hero_job_tip: Find out whether results mean closing a deal or delivering the project, and whether you can work on the physical solution.

EAR.headline: Get support for a proposal so it can actually happen
EAR.scene: Finding someone to provide space, funding, and time may be the part you most want to own. Show different ways to explain what the project would do, then use a sample to make the trade-offs in size, materials, or assembly visible.
EAR.career_lens: For creative roles with a business development focus, ask what counts as getting a project off the ground: signing a partner, delivering a proposal, or producing a usable sample. Different people often own each milestone.
EAR.question: After an agreement, can the person who started it decide what to show and check a sample, or do the design and production teams take over?
EAR.trial: Write two partnership terms for an imaginary market. Make a one-page proposal and test part of a stall layout with paper.
EAR.decision: If you liked getting a partner on board, look for roles responsible for adoption. If preparing the proposal or building the sample appealed more, look for clear ownership of that output.
EAR.screen: Determine whether the job mainly wins partners, sets the proposal's direction, or makes a sample people can see. Ask who owns each part.
EAR.hero_job_tip: Compare how much time goes into securing resources, creating a proposal, and taking part in a trial build.

activity_chain: Observe through three separate activity entry points: work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions; try different approaches to expression, style, narrative, or form; organize rules, data, processes, order, or reviewable records.

positive_value: The value of this content is to break the clues into observable small tasks: Realistic focuses on tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results; Artistic focuses on expression, style, narrative, form, and experience; Conventional focuses on rules, data, processes, order, and reviewable records. Whichever comes first only indicates which activity to gather evidence from first. These clues offer exploration questions, not job answers.
real_world_cost: Reading boundary: these three clues may occur in different parts of one task or across different environments. Record only the appeal of specific activities, points of hesitation, and conditions you want to adjust. Do not turn the score order into a ranking of abilities or a fixed way of working.
first_experiment: Spend 30 minutes on a low-risk observation: in the first 10 minutes, bring materials, equipment, samples, or on-site constraints into view; in the next 10 minutes, try expression, naming, rewriting, layout, or a choice of form; in the final 10 minutes, clearly organize the steps, fields, rules, or records of checks. Record only which action you most want to continue.
low_risk_validation: Low-risk observation: choose a small task that accommodates hands-on, expression, and process clues. Record the three activities separately and look only at activity preferences and evidence of wanting to continue.
primary_activity_chain: Start with the first dimension, Realistic: use it as the initial observation entry point and look for small-task evidence involving tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results.
secondary_support_line: Then consider the second dimension, Artistic: use it as an additional observation entry point and record whether expression, style, narrative, form, and experience make the task more appealing.
tertiary_stabilizer: The third dimension, Conventional, is only an additional clue: observe whether rules, data, processes, order, and reviewable records help distinguish more specific task conditions.

The order changes what to ask first and what to validate next. It is not a fixed identity, an ability conclusion, or a career answer.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make a prototype possible to reproduce
desktop_reading_v1.scene: A display stand looks good but is hard to reassemble at each site. Revise the joint and the appearance, then document measurements and acceptance checks.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Find out whether the prototype role owns its appearance, construction, and handover specifications or mainly builds to a drawing.
desktop_reading_v1.question: After a design changes, who turns the revised sample into specifications and acceptance checks others can use?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Make a folding model from paper. Draw the assembly steps and try building it again from your instructions alone.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want to make new samples, look closely at the prototype work. If you also want to keep production consistent, compare process and quality roles.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Prototyping a product and maintaining its specifications can both require knowing the material. Ask whether you can change its construction and appearance or mostly check whether finished items meet the existing specifications.

RAC.headline: Make something attractive that others can reproduce
RAC.scene: You might want to build a sample that works. After choosing its shape and finish, document the dimensions and assembly steps that affect the appearance so the next one can match.
RAC.career_lens: Some production jobs let you adjust appearance while building. Others follow a finished design. Ask what you can change on one actual sample, what you have to document, and whether someone else can reproduce it.
RAC.question: When a sample's outline changed at the last minute, did a newcomer rebuild it from the drawing or also update the drawing and version record?
RAC.trial: Make two paper holders. Change the outline of the first and write a dimensions-and-steps card to see if it can be reproduced in the second.
RAC.decision: If you want to keep testing materials and making things, prioritize production. If appearance or repeatability mattered more, check who owns the design or maintains the specifications.
RAC.screen: Check weekly production time, how much you can change the presentation, and whether you document specifications so someone can build it again.
RAC.hero_job_tip: Ask how much time goes to prototyping and who sets the form and the production specifications.

RCA.headline: Refine a repeated task at the workbench
RCA.scene: You might enjoy working with tools and materials directly. Rearrange parts people keep picking up by mistake, record the right order, and change the labels so others can find what they need at a glance.
RCA.career_lens: Some fabrication and assembly jobs mainly deliver consistent, traceable work. If you also want to contribute to design, ask whether you can propose a new fixture when one doesn't work well or only record the exception.
RCA.question: If an item meets its specifications and is still hard to use, can a newcomer propose changing the structure or only document the issue and pass it on?
RCA.trial: Make three paper parts to one size and list the checks for acceptance. If one is hard to handle, sketch a change that preserves the important dimensions.
RCA.decision: If you want to repeat the work and check it against specifications, look at production roles. If you mainly want to change the structure, check who owns those design decisions.
RCA.screen: Mark duties that work to specifications and record deviations. Ask whether you can propose smaller design changes within those rules.
RCA.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you mainly operate equipment or maintain standards, and whether you can improve the workstation or its instructions.

ARC.headline: Make a design ready to build and deliver
ARC.scene: You might care most about the form, proportions, and feel of different materials. Build a sample to inspect the seams, then put the details that matter into the specifications so the piece retains its character after handover.
ARC.career_lens: A job that turns concepts into reproducible small runs can involve trial builds, refining the appearance, and writing specifications. Ask whether you decide how it looks and stay involved in testing production after the design is approved.
ARC.question: After the design is approved, does a newcomer check a second build and revise the dimensional notes?
ARC.trial: Sketch two shapes for a paper nameplate and make one of them. Write three specifications and ask someone to reproduce it from the instructions.
ARC.decision: If you want to try another form, look for design ownership. If adjustment or consistency interested you more, compare time in production and keeping specifications current.
ARC.screen: Look for creative roles that design the form, make the first item, and provide reproducible specifications. Distinguish concept work from production handover.
ARC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can refine the design alongside the prototype and whether you set or follow the delivery requirements.

ACR.headline: Turn a visual approach into standards the next person can use
ACR.scene: You might enjoy setting the layout and colors for a packaging range. Give the different sizes a shared labeling system, then check the first physical production run to see which design details still need work.
ACR.career_lens: A visual project may involve deciding proportions, colors, and layouts or mainly managing versions and material specifications. Ask whether checking a physical sample on site is also part of the job.
ACR.question: When a template is used on a new material, can the designer adjust the rule and verify a sample?
ACR.trial: Make two signs for the same topic, with rules for type size and numbering. View them at different distances and note which specification should change.
ACR.decision: If choosing how to present things mattered most, look for creative discretion. If you also want to maintain standards and inspect physical samples, check for both responsibilities.
ACR.screen: Compare design choices with maintaining standards. Ask whether you can take a sample to the actual site and check it there.
ACR.hero_job_tip: Check whether the job lets you set design principles, maintain the standards, and help build the physical sample.

CRA.headline: Straighten out a process that keeps going wrong
CRA.scene: You might want each step to have a standard others can check. Verify where tools sit and how each step is performed at the workbench. Then choose a clearer diagram for the handover.
CRA.career_lens: Acceptance checks bring together the physical item, work order, and specifications. If you also want to make the documentation easier to use, find out whether you could redraw labels or checklists and personally inspect parts that failed.
CRA.question: If handover records and item labels disagree, can a newcomer check the site and remake the labels?
CRA.trial: Make an inventory checklist for a box of stationery, inspect each item, and redraw the label that would be easiest to put in the wrong place.
CRA.decision: If you want to keep inspecting and documenting items, start with quality or inventory roles. If changing a label was more appealing, check for information design duties.
CRA.screen: Look for jobs that check lists and sign off deliveries. Find out whether you inspect the physical items and improve labels people confuse.
CRA.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you inspect to a standard or also take part on site and change how instructions are presented.

CAR.headline: Build an operating standard people will actually use
CAR.scene: You might catch the same rule written differently in three documents. Bring the reference numbers and versions into line, make a visual guide for the key steps, and walk through it beside the equipment to see what needs changing.
CAR.career_lens: In records or standards management, you might make a diagram others can act on. Ask whether you only issue new versions or also check signs and samples on site and revise the instructions when something doesn't match.
CAR.question: When an instruction and the physical item show different versions for the same reference number, can this role inspect the item and revise the guidance?
CAR.trial: Organize five objects by category and sketch where to find them. Verify the drawing, reference numbers, and physical locations one by one.
CAR.decision: If maintaining clear rules appealed most, start with records or standards. If you preferred drawing instructions or inspecting items, compare how much time those take.
CAR.screen: Look for version control, classification, and maintaining standards. Check whether you also make visual instructions and can verify them in person.
CAR.hero_job_tip: In process roles, find out who manages documents, designs instructions, and checks the work in person.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Help people get something working on site
desktop_reading_v1.scene: An event is about to start. Equipment isn't ready and volunteers aren't sure what to do. The work can involve adjusting the equipment, showing people how to use it, and changing who handles what.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Find out whether the role focuses on working on site, training people, or being accountable for the schedule and coordination.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When something goes wrong before an event, does someone in this role diagnose the equipment problem and help beginners, or mostly coordinate the response?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Pick a familiar everyday tool. Make a quick-start card and assign on-site responsibilities for a small group task.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want to guide a team without spending most days responding to emergencies, ask how often unplanned work comes up and how teams hand it over.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Event operations, service coordination, and equipment operation can appear in one posting. Find out whether the role mainly solves on-site problems, coaches new people, or schedules resources to get the work done.

RSE.headline: Finish the job and show teammates how to do it
RSE.scene: You might first want to fit the troublesome part on site. Let the person taking over try it once. If they need a shared tool that isn't available, talk to the person responsible about access and timing.
RSE.career_lens: Some on-site service shifts focus on equipment checks. Others also help visitors through practical difficulties while operating it. Ask whether you refer problems beyond your authority or contact the people who can resolve them.
RSE.question: When a tool becomes unavailable, does a newcomer handle the equipment and help visitors? Who handles issues beyond their authority?
RSE.trial: Set up a tabletop service desk. Ask someone to simulate having trouble collecting an item, clear the obstacle, and agree on a backup plan.
RSE.decision: If you want to solve hands-on problems, keep roles centered on operations. If serving people or coordinating appealed more, find out how regularly those tasks come up.
RSE.screen: Mark operating equipment and troubleshooting in person. See whether you also help visitors directly or arrange other staff.
RSE.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can both operate equipment and teach others to use it. Find out how much coordination you would own.

RES.headline: Get an on-site change through handover
RES.scene: You might prefer fixing a fault you can handle yourself. After the repair, agree when teams can switch equipment. Ask the next shift to operate it while you watch for any step that still needs a reminder.
RES.career_lens: When a service moves to a new site, you might install and test equipment, arrange handover, and set aside time for users to practice. Find out if you deliver working equipment or stay until people are ready to take it over.
RES.question: After equipment is working, must a newcomer arrange the handover and run through operation with users before the job is complete?
RES.trial: Rearrange a shared item, make time to try it, and show someone how to use it. Write down what you missed in the handover.
RES.decision: If you want to set things up and hand them over, look at implementation roles. If you preferred arranging the trial or teaching others, check the time those duties get.
RES.screen: See what an implementation job installs or adjusts directly. Ask whether handover and helping people get started are part of acceptance.
RES.hero_job_tip: Find out how far you would take a repair yourself and whether you would also coordinate downtime or training.

SRE.headline: Help a team start using a new tool
SRE.scene: You might care most about whether everyone can use a tool independently. Listen to what confuses them, practice with them, then talk to a supervisor about setting time aside for practice.
SRE.career_lens: For community facilities or activity support, ask for one example of a request for help. Did the person in the role explain how to use something, go on site and adjust it, or coordinate with others to remove an obstacle? Where the task ends tells you what the work involves.
SRE.question: If someone can't use the event equipment easily, can a newcomer try a different layout with them? Who can help with resources?
SRE.trial: Have someone try to pick up items from a shared desk. Listen, remove one obstacle, and agree on who will maintain the new setup.
SRE.decision: If you want to follow up with the person, keep direct support jobs. If you preferred fixing the setup or coordinating the response, check who owns those tasks.
SRE.screen: Find work that helps participants in person. See whether an obstacle calls for changing the setup or getting other people involved.
SRE.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you would teach on site and whether you'd need to get training time or equipment approved.

SER.headline: Arrange the support a group needs
SER.scene: You might notice that new colleagues keep asking for help with one step they haven't practiced. Pull together what they say, get some training time approved, and work through the step with them and the actual tools.
SER.career_lens: In service project coordination, find out whether you hear directly what participants need. Then ask if you decide how to allocate support or rearrange seating, equipment, or access on site. These responsibilities can belong to separate teams.
SER.question: When a participant explains a difficulty, can this role arrange help or make changes on site, or can it only respond to them?
SER.trial: Plan a tabletop activity for someone. Ask what they need, agree how you can help, and try setting the activity up.
SER.decision: If you want ongoing contact with participants, keep jobs combining service and coordination. If you most enjoy getting the setup right, look at event operations.
SER.screen: Look for direct service and arranging resources. Find out whether you also prepare the venue or equipment.
SER.hero_job_tip: Compare time spent supporting employees directly and securing commitments across departments. Ask if you can demonstrate on site.

ERS.headline: Negotiate a workable plan for an on-site improvement
ERS.scene: You might prefer getting several groups to make an improvement possible. Walk the person responsible through the equipment change, then arrange a handover that leaves the people using it time to learn.
ERS.career_lens: For on-site project work, distinguish organizing staff, building the setup, and solving problems participants encounter. When the venue changed at short notice, did this role reschedule and assign work or also get equipment in place and restore the service?
ERS.question: After the last venue change, did a newcomer reschedule staff, help set up, or mainly notify people?
ERS.trial: Pretend the venue has shrunk by half. Reassign two duties, set up a small help point, and ask someone to try the route.
ERS.decision: If you want to follow the changes through on site, look for coordination authority and access to outcomes. If hands-on setup or helping participants mattered most, seek out that primary responsibility.
ERS.screen: Find jobs that explicitly assign on-site duties and resources. Check whether the coordinator physically helps set up or works directly with participants.
ERS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the role ends at agreeing on plans and results or also involves carrying them out and coaching people afterward.

ESR.headline: Get people to adopt a new on-site procedure
ESR.scene: You might be drawn to getting several shifts to agree to try a new procedure. Find out what support operators need, demonstrate the equipment, and use their feedback to plan what happens next with a supervisor.
ESR.career_lens: Find out whether people leading projects on the front line can use feedback to arrange resources. Some mainly recruit and coordinate; others check the equipment and space in person and make changes happen.
ESR.question: After staffing is sorted, does a newcomer have time to hear what participants need and change the setup?
ESR.trial: Ask someone to pose two participant needs. Negotiate one workable arrangement and draw the visitor route to see if it accommodates them.
ESR.decision: If securing help and making the plan work appealed most, keep jobs with real coordination responsibility. If participant requests or physical changes drew you in, check the time given to those tasks.
ESR.screen: Compare recruitment and staffing duties, then ask whether you can hear directly from participants and help make on-site changes.
ESR.hero_job_tip: Check whether your main responsibility is getting people to adopt a practice, and whether you would work directly with users and equipment.
