desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make on-site work easy to hand over
desktop_reading_v1.scene: New colleagues understand the procedure and still skip the final check. Show them how to do it, leave a checklist, and observe what people still miss after training.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Look at operating equipment, coaching people, and keeping records. Identify which activity you want to do regularly.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When can someone new usually operate on their own? How often do you update checklists in response to what happens on site?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Make a five-step handover card for a familiar, safe task. Ask a colleague to explain the steps using the card.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If demonstrating and correcting a mistake appealed most, look first at coaching duties. If you wanted to establish a consistent standard, look at process responsibilities.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: On-site coaching can center on demonstrating a procedure or on reviewing records. Compare postings that explicitly mention coaching beginners in person, making checklists, or updating operating instructions.

RSC.headline: Teach on-site operations well enough for a confident handover
RSC.scene: You might like work where you have tools in your hands and can see the result. Demonstrate an inspection to a newcomer, explain safety limits while they practice, and note easily missed checks on the handover sheet.
RSC.career_lens: For equipment or facility operations, ask whether you check and fix things yourself. If you also train newcomers, find out whether you demonstrate occasionally or are responsible for independent operation and updating the handover checklist.
RSC.question: From shadowing to independent work, who demonstrates, verifies a newcomer's work, and updates the records?
RSC.trial: Organize some stationery, inspect it, and show someone how to repeat the process. Write a three-line checklist of what they missed.
RSC.decision: If you want to keep doing the task directly, look for field operations. If you want to teach or improve the checklist, look for real time in those tasks.
RSC.screen: Find jobs with hands-on inspections or operation, and mark whether you also demonstrate procedures and fill out handover checks.
RSC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the job combines operating equipment with training others, and which records you update each shift.

RCS.headline: Finish the hands-on work and leave the key steps for the next shift
RCS.scene: Once you have checked an item, can the next person tell immediately what needs to happen? The handover may be part of what interests you. Mark what needs rework against a shared standard, then check it together on site so the next shift can see what the checklist means.
RCS.career_lens: Operating roles need records. Ask how much of a shift goes to keeping them and whether they're an aid or the main output. If you want to pass on field experience, check for time to train colleagues or revise instructions.
RCS.question: If the record passed but the equipment looks wrong, does a newcomer check it personally and explain it to the next shift?
RCS.trial: Assemble a paper model, check three items on a list, and show someone how to use the list to check the finished model.
RCS.decision: If both building and checking appealed, keep field roles with clear handover duties. If you wanted to explain it to others, check how much training you get to do.
RCS.screen: Compare time operating equipment and keeping itemized records. Check whether you teach people to follow the process.
RCS.hero_job_tip: Find out how an ordinary day splits between hands-on tasks, checklist checks, and training whoever takes over.

SRC.headline: Coach someone until they can operate independently
SRC.scene: You might care most about the moment someone no longer needs help. Let them practice with real tools and put the easy-to-miss checks on one list for them to use afterward.
SRC.career_lens: Ask what a training role delivers after a session. If it includes demonstrating, coaching, recording progress, and handing over steps people still need help with, your work continues beyond the initial explanation.
SRC.question: How does a coach know a learner can work independently? Do newcomers get to demonstrate and record progress?
SRC.trial: Teach someone a familiar craft and let them do it alone. Record where they needed a prompt and where they didn't.
SRC.decision: If you want to coach another round, prioritize practical training. If making the object or recording progress mattered more, find roles where that is central.
SRC.screen: Find jobs that coach people directly. Check whether you demonstrate in person and record progress.
SRC.hero_job_tip: Ask who sets up repeated practice, provides actual equipment, and tracks progress in a coaching role.

SCR.headline: Make sure anyone who asks for help gets follow-up
SCR.scene: Support is hard to continue if someone has to tell the same story every time they ask for help. You might want to track where they struggle and how far they have practiced. At the next session, you can open the record and start at the step they couldn't get past.
SCR.career_lens: Service follow-up often involves recording who handles a case next. Ask whether you can show people how to use the real object as well as answering questions and updating records, or mostly work by phone with existing instructions.
SCR.question: When a request needs follow-up across shifts, can a newcomer demonstrate a solution? What information goes into the handover?
SCR.trial: Ask someone for a question about a familiar tool. Demonstrate the answer and leave a note a colleague could use to continue helping.
SCR.decision: If you want to keep answering and following up, explore support. If clear handovers or field operations appealed more, compare time spent on each.
SCR.screen: Find jobs that answer questions and maintain follow-up records. Ask whether you sometimes demonstrate with the real equipment.
SCR.hero_job_tip: In a support job, compare how much time goes into follow-up, record keeping, and demonstrating a task on site.

CRS.headline: Give operations and handovers standards people can follow
CRS.scene: You might pay attention to whether people on the next shift can see what the current shift did. Walk through the task, choose the checks that must be recorded, and teach a newcomer how to fill in and verify the record.
CRS.career_lens: For store handover or equipment management, a good result means the physical items, system records, and next person's understanding match. Find out whether you spend most days checking items or also turn gaps you find into steps for training the next shift.
CRS.question: When an inventory check finds conflicting records, does this role verify on site and show the next shift what to check?
CRS.trial: Count five items using a checklist. Pick an unclear instruction, check it together, and revise the record.
CRS.decision: If matching records to physical items was appealing, keep inventory or quality handover jobs. If you want to teach on site, ask about coaching new colleagues.
CRS.screen: Look for inspections and records. Check whether you verify the items in person and coach the next shift or mainly check the system.
CRS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you help set the standard and how much time goes to on-site verification and coaching newcomers.

CSR.headline: Organize a service so support continues when another person takes over
CSR.scene: If the handover omits what a learner has tried, the next colleague has to ask them from the beginning. You could clarify the record so somebody else can keep helping. If the problem needs showing, bring the actual equipment.
CSR.career_lens: For a service process role, ask who sets intake rules and who helps people who get stuck trying to follow them. When registration causes problems, find out whether you adjust the equipment on site or hand it to operations.
CSR.question: When people repeatedly ask for help at the same step, can you change the checklist and try the new procedure with users on site?
CSR.trial: Write borrowing and return rules for shared stationery. Ask someone to try them, handle one exception, and change part of the layout.
CSR.decision: If keeping the rules clear appeals, look at process work. If helping people in person was more interesting, find out how the role reaches actual users.
CSR.screen: Find roles that manage verification procedures. Ask whether they also work with users and can change how equipment is arranged.
CSR.hero_job_tip: Check whether you mainly deliver reliable records or practice with people directly and how much of either involves working on site.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Follow the plan through to on-site delivery
desktop_reading_v1.scene: An order changes at short notice before the sample is accepted. Someone checks the item, someone rearranges the schedule, and someone records the changes so shifts can use the same checklist.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Identify who fixes problems on site, who can reschedule delivery, and who owns the standards and change log.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When delivery ran late last time, could this role revise the schedule or inspection method, or did it mainly update the status?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Pick a real handover with no sensitive information. Write a step each for checking the work, changing the order, and recording what changed.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If coordinating was most appealing, check whether the role can set priorities. If you wanted to make the handover reliable, check whether you can change the process.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Project delivery and quality management can both include final acceptance. Project delivery often involves resolving delays and assigning responsibilities. Quality management checks that the physical work and the records agree.

REC.headline: Carry an equipment upgrade through to on-site delivery
REC.scene: You might want to fix a device that keeps failing. The machine needs downtime, so agree on a window with production and document the replacement parts and acceptance checks.
REC.career_lens: When an implementation job owns delivery, ask whether you personally install or configure equipment, and whether you can reschedule if there is a conflict. Check whether you document tests, omissions, and sign-off or hand over once installation is done.
REC.question: When the last installation ran out of time, could a newcomer rearrange tasks and document acceptance criteria?
REC.trial: Use paper parts to simulate assembly. If something is missing, change the order and write a handover record the next shift can verify.
REC.decision: If building was most engaging, look for jobs with hands-on time. If scheduling or checking delivery appealed more, ask what authority the role has.
REC.screen: Check whether you carry out installations yourself. Find out whether rescheduling people and accepting the delivery are core duties or things you help with.
REC.hero_job_tip: Start with roles that own physical changes. Ask how much time then goes to coordinating downtime and documenting acceptance.

RCE.headline: Make every repair traceable
RCE.scene: You might want to restore a machine against clear standards. If the same part keeps failing, record readings before and after each repair, then use those findings to discuss a replacement or upgrade.
RCE.career_lens: For fixture, facility, or equipment improvement jobs, ask what you modify yourself. Some also update operating records and ask the team to try a new approach. If the focus is promoting adoption, the hands-on component can be smaller than the title suggests.
RCE.question: The last time a shop-floor change became a procedure, who made it, documented it, and persuaded the next shift to try it?
RCE.trial: Rearrange a set of tools and write three rules for putting them back. Ask someone to try them and point out one rule that doesn't work.
RCE.decision: If you want hands-on work and fewer repeated mistakes, keep field jobs with handover ownership. If getting others to adopt changes appealed more, look for roles that own that work.
RCE.screen: Look for jobs with hands-on checks and adjustments and responsibility for handover rules. Ask whether you also help others adopt the changes.
RCE.hero_job_tip: Find out who owns routine maintenance, handles exceptions, and requests upgrades.

ERC.headline: Turn requests from several sites into one upgrade the team can deliver
ERC.scene: Several shifts want the equipment upgraded and none wants to give up production time. You might be most drawn to getting those groups to agree. Use a sample modification to show the plan and agree on the acceptance and handover rules.
ERC.career_lens: For project delivery, ask who negotiates dates and who resolves on-site problems. If you want to work with equipment or materials, use a recent handover to see whether you would inspect the physical work or collect signatures and follow up on progress.
ERC.question: When delivery dates conflict, can the lead reassign responsibility? Does acceptance mean inspecting the work or collecting signatures?
ERC.trial: Simulate a tabletop installation. Agree on who does what and by when, handle one part, and check it against agreed conditions.
ERC.decision: If you want to own the commitment and see the result on site, keep coordination roles with acceptance duties. If you prefer installation or checking, look for that core responsibility.
ERC.screen: Mark jobs that coordinate staff to meet a deadline. Ask whether they also set up and inspect work on site.
ERC.hero_job_tip: In project roles, ask whether you negotiate downtime, budgets, and responsibilities and whether you follow test fits on site.

ECR.headline: Turn an agreed goal into a delivery everyone can verify
ECR.scene: You may be drawn to getting several parties behind the same goal. Once you agree on who's responsible and when it is due, put the commitments on an acceptance checklist and see whether the installed equipment meets it in person.
ECR.career_lens: For delivery management jobs, find out whether performance is judged on securing commitments up front or documenting delivery and acceptance at the end. If you want contact with the equipment itself, ask whether you can go on site to check a disputed delivery.
ECR.question: The last time a supplier was late, could a newcomer renegotiate the deadline, update acceptance conditions, and verify the delivery on site?
ECR.trial: Imagine two shipments will arrive late. Agree on priorities with someone, write one page of responsibilities and acceptance checks, and run through it with objects on a desk.
ECR.decision: If following through on commitments was the part you wanted to own, keep jobs with coordination and sign-off responsibilities. If you mainly wanted to document or inspect the delivery, look for roles that make room for those duties.
ECR.screen: Check who sets the order of work and who signs off. Look separately at commitments, acceptance rules, and on-site verification.
ECR.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the job centers on reaching agreement or also includes setting acceptance rules and joining on-site checks.

CRE.headline: Use inspection records to drive equipment improvements
CRE.scene: How many repairs were made, and which one worked? You might want to make each inspection traceable. Once you check the equipment on site against the same standard, the records give you something concrete to discuss with the person deciding which repairs come first.
CRE.career_lens: A quality role can decide whether work meets a standard or follow up to get it corrected. Ask whether you inspect physical items and coordinate a fix when the same issue comes up repeatedly.
CRE.question: Who noticed a required item missing from the maintenance form? Could a newcomer inspect the equipment and get the form changed?
CRE.trial: Make an equipment repair form and run two items through it. Find a gap and propose a change to the form.
CRE.decision: If you want to make records easy to verify, consider process quality. If you want to change equipment or coordinate corrective work, check access to the site and authority to propose changes.
CRE.screen: Look for roles that maintain checklists, inspect equipment, and request corrections. Distinguish completing the form from being able to change it.
CRE.hero_job_tip: In inspection or quality roles, ask whether you help design the checks and how far you can follow up on what you find.

CER.headline: Check who owes what and what actually got delivered
CER.scene: You might want to reconcile what the contract, work order, and acceptance record each say. After seeing the condition of the equipment, you can confirm what is incomplete and which party can arrange the fix.
CER.career_lens: Writing intake and acceptance rules takes time, and so does getting everyone to follow them. If you want both duties, ask who negotiates revised dates with suppliers and when you would verify results on site.
CER.question: When a delivery misses the acceptance criteria, can a newcomer reset deadlines and responsibilities, or do they only record the exception? Would they recheck the item in person?
CER.trial: Write three standards for a desk setup, agree on when changes are due, and then check the setup against each standard and record the exceptions.
CER.decision: If you want to set clear rules and follow up on them, keep roles that combine standards maintenance with coordination. If you also want hands-on work, ask how much is done on site.
CER.screen: Look for jobs that maintain standards and coordinate their use. Check whether you would personally re-inspect what is being signed off.
CER.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you mainly track records or can also request corrective work and verify the result on site.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Find the cause and turn it into something people can use
desktop_reading_v1.scene: Several new hires say the guide is hard to follow. After watching people use it twice, you see they're looking for a button the instructions never identify. Break the procedure into three images and circle the entry point. The next person can finish on their own. This work gives you a chance to investigate, explain, and see what people do with the result.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare what you would deliver most often: evidence, visual or written materials, or helping people learn a task. Similar job titles can have very different mixes.
desktop_reading_v1.question: After the last time users got stuck, did a newcomer get to observe, revise the instructions, or follow up to see what users learned?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Pick a public guide. Find one step that could be misunderstood, write one sentence explaining why, and draw a clearer version.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you most want to check the evidence, look for direct access to source material. If you want to improve the explanation or see someone learn the task, look for access to feedback.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Research jobs deliver findings people can check. Content jobs deliver materials people can understand. Teaching jobs also need to see what people learn to do. Similar titles can put the emphasis in different places.

IAS.headline: Get to the bottom of a problem that keeps coming back
IAS.scene: New hires have read the guide, yet they keep stopping at the same step. You might first want to know where they get stuck. Watch a few people try it and notice they all mistake the same button for the starting point. Turn the instructions into a diagram and see whether the next new hire can get through on their own.
IAS.career_lens: Compare what research, content, and teaching roles deliver: a conclusion others can check, instructions a reader can use, or a task a learner can perform independently. Start with jobs where you can investigate the cause and see how people use the findings.
IAS.question: The last time users got stuck at the same step, what evidence did a newcomer check? After the change was tried, who checked whether it solved the problem?
IAS.trial: Pick a public guide and ask someone to try one step. Note where they got stuck and what you observed, revise one instruction, and test it again.
IAS.decision: If you want to keep digging into why people got stuck, favor jobs with direct access to source material. If revising the instructions or helping people get started was more interesting, check whether those tasks recur in the job.
IAS.screen: Mark the postings that give you access to original material and a chance to investigate where users struggle. Then note whether the role delivers findings, revises instructions, or follows people through onboarding.
IAS.hero_job_tip: Start with roles where you can observe users directly and investigate problems. Ask whether you can help revise the guide once the findings are in.

ISA.headline: Find out why everyone asks for help at the same step
ISA.scene: Three people say the guide is confusing. You might ask whether they are all running into the same issue. Hear each person describe what they did, separate the different causes behind similar problems, and use that to improve the examples.
ISA.career_lens: In user research or learning evaluation, look for access to first-hand material and the chance to investigate recurring problems. Ask whether you hear where participants got stuck and whether you deliver findings alone or turn them into something people can use.
ISA.question: After several similar requests come in, can a newcomer follow up to confirm the cause? Who turns the findings into clearer guidance?
ISA.trial: Group three public requests for help and identify one possible cause. Have someone explain their understanding back to you, then draw a visual prompt.
ISA.decision: If you want to keep investigating and hear from users, look for research with follow-up. If you prefer making something from the findings, find out who decides what the material looks like.
ISA.screen: Look for work that investigates difficulties people share. Find out whether you stay in touch with people or turn findings into materials.
ISA.hero_job_tip: Look for roles with access to original support requests and a chance to verify what happened with users.

AIS.headline: Find a clearer way to present something people struggle to understand
AIS.scene: You could turn the same beginner's guide into a diagram or a short demonstration. You might most enjoy deciding what people see first. Compare both versions with new users, then revise the one that helps them follow the steps.
AIS.career_lens: When looking at content and design jobs, first find out whether you decide what readers see and how they see it. Compare assignments where you rewrite existing material with jobs where you can check the facts, get readers to try it, and revise the presentation.
AIS.question: On the last revision, could a newcomer use feedback to compare two versions they made, or did they simply follow the review notes?
AIS.trial: Pick a publicly documented step. Make a diagram and a short demonstration. Ask someone to try both and note which leaves fewer pauses.
AIS.decision: If you want to try another format, look for control over revisions and access to feedback. If finding the cause or coaching appeals more, check how much working time goes to those duties.
AIS.screen: Find out who decides how to present information and whether the creator can check facts and test it with users.
AIS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can choose how to present the information and revise it in response to what people actually do.

ASI.headline: Turn an idea into something people can learn
ASI.scene: You might want to turn a dense rule into a practice exercise with a recognizable situation. Walk a newcomer through it and listen to how they interpret it. If several people miss the same line, check whether the explanation or the task itself is getting in the way.
ASI.career_lens: If you want to design training people will use, find out who chooses the exercises and how to teach them. Check whether you can observe learners and use practice results or feedback to figure out what they missed. That tells you who owns the learning experience.
ASI.question: Once a course is released, can a newcomer observe a practice session and change the order of the material in response to what learners do?
ASI.trial: Turn a familiar task into a three-minute illustrated guide and do it once with someone. Note which explanation was hardest to follow, revise it, and ask them to explain it back.
ASI.decision: If you want to keep breaking down and arranging the content, look for jobs that include design and trial sessions. If you preferred coaching or investigating a misunderstanding, check which jobs give those tasks real time.
ASI.screen: Look for jobs where you can choose examples and sequence exercises. Check whether you work directly with learners and investigate which steps they haven't mastered.
ASI.hero_job_tip: Find out whether content creators also get to explain the material, lead practice, and make revisions based on what learners actually do.

SIA.headline: Trace why someone couldn't get the hang of a task
SIA.scene: You might care most about whether a new colleague can do the task back at their desk. Listen to why they stopped, compare that with the difficulties others reported, and rewrite the prompt in a form that addresses the actual problem.
SIA.career_lens: Look separately at helping people directly and investigating behind the scenes. When someone is stuck at the same step again, do you help them continue or investigate why multiple people get stuck? A role that turns findings into new guidance also involves creating materials.
SIA.question: When several people struggle with the same task, does a newcomer have time to follow cases, investigate the shared problem, and revise the help material?
SIA.trial: Ask someone about a recent difficulty learning a task. Ask two questions to clarify what happened and sketch a prompt they can use immediately.
SIA.decision: If you want to stay with someone and see their progress, keep ongoing support roles. If you most want to find a common cause, look for access to original feedback.
SIA.screen: Start with jobs that answer questions or coach people directly. Find out whether you can investigate similar problems and turn the findings into visual materials.
SIA.hero_job_tip: Look for roles that let you follow up with learners. Ask whether you can investigate repeated difficulties and who revises the materials.

SAI.headline: Find another way to help someone get started
SAI.scene: If someone reads the guide and still hesitates to try, you might want to sit beside them. Use a different picture or show the steps until they can do it themselves. Check back later to see which support they actually used.
SAI.career_lens: A coaching role may let you rewrite the tutorial, try a new demonstration, and see whether people learned. If the job is mainly measured by how many sessions you complete, check whether it gives you time for those tasks.
SAI.question: After coaching someone, can a newcomer rewrite an example and watch them try again?
SAI.trial: Help someone with a small, safe task. Change one prompt and have them repeat it. Note whether they ask one fewer question.
SAI.decision: If you want to keep practicing with people, look for coaching time. If creating materials or checking what worked was more interesting, look for jobs that deliver those outputs.
SAI.screen: Look for regular hands-on coaching with room to change explanations. Ask whether the team checks how well people work on their own before and after a change.
SAI.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you usually coach people directly or deliver material, and whether you have time to check what learners retained.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make a discovery into a proposal people will try
desktop_reading_v1.scene: Use of a feature is dropping. A team can find out whether access changed or whether people no longer need it as much. Then it can sketch two versions of the instructions and make the case for a trial to the person who sets the schedule.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare jobs by whether the main task is gathering evidence, working out how to present it, or getting another team to adopt a change.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When you find an opportunity, can one person investigate why it exists, illustrate a solution, and request a trial?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Use a public example to propose two explanations. Draw a way to explain the situation and write one reason to run a trial.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want to keep investigating why something happened, check how much time goes to research. If making a pilot happen interests you too, look at who owns implementation.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Strategy roles may combine analysis, drafting proposals, and securing resources. Ask whether you can take part in the investigation and whether you would own a pilot or business outcome at the end.

IAE.headline: Bring the findings into the decision
IAE.scene: You might want to investigate why users abandoned one step. Check the records, turn different explanations into diagrams the team can compare, and discuss how to get a chance to test them.
IAE.career_lens: In strategy roles, ask whether analysis can shape the proposal or simply supports a direction already agreed. Find out how evidence gets into the proposal, who decides how to present it, and whether you also ask for a pilot.
IAE.question: If evidence doesn't support the original idea, can a newcomer revise the proposal and join the pilot discussion?
IAE.trial: Check an idea for improvement against public material. Make a one-page proposal with visuals and explain to someone why a small trial is worth doing.
IAE.decision: If you want to keep following the evidence, look for investigative scope. If preparing a proposal or convincing decision-makers appealed more, add those responsibilities to your criteria.
IAE.screen: Look for strategy jobs where you can verify the evidence. Mark who turns it into a proposal and who asks for a pilot.
IAE.hero_job_tip: Prioritize roles where you can verify evidence yourself and get the findings into the next decision.

IEA.headline: Build a decision on evidence people can verify
IEA.scene: A manager is ready to add staff, but the delay only happens at one time of day. You might want to see whether the issue is staffing or overlapping handovers. Bring possible changes to a pilot discussion and use a clear chart to show what is disputed.
IEA.career_lens: Some strategy jobs use research to change decisions. Others spend more time reconciling different demands. Ask who did the analysis, negotiated commitments, and structured the materials in a project that was implemented.
IEA.question: Once a report is done, does a newcomer help agree on pilot conditions? Who decides how to present the findings?
IEA.trial: Compare two options using fictional data. Identify one finding that could affect the decision, ask someone to agree to a trial, and make a visual summary.
IEA.decision: If you want to gather more evidence and talk through trade-offs, look for roles with room for both. If research itself appealed more, check how much time goes to negotiation.
IEA.screen: Compare access to data and choices over analysis. Find out whether the role then coordinates resources, prepares an explanation, or does both.
IEA.hero_job_tip: Ask whether research briefs document decisions already taken or whether you can change the team's direction with evidence.

AIE.headline: Show how a new approach works and what supports it
AIE.scene: A different diagram can make the same proposal easier to understand. You might want to develop two versions, check that both convey the same essential information, and choose one to take to a trial discussion.
AIE.career_lens: If you want to contribute creative work to strategy, ask whether you can study the audience before developing ideas. After testing a way to explain something, find out whether you revise it from evidence or also go to a review to ask for a pilot.
AIE.question: What material can a newcomer use to test a creative idea early on? Who stays responsible after approval?
AIE.trial: Sketch two promotions for one event. Revise one using public information about the audience, then ask someone which they would try.
AIE.decision: If reworking how the idea is presented mattered most, look for creative ownership and a chance to verify it. If getting backing appealed more, check who moves the proposal forward.
AIE.screen: Look for roles that shape the proposal. Find out whether the creator studies the audience and requests time for a trial.
AIE.hero_job_tip: Look for time to develop and test materials. Ask whose support you would need to get a proposal adopted.

AEI.headline: Present a good idea so people are willing to try it
AEI.scene: You might want to try several ways to present a proposal so people see immediately what they would get. Listen for the decision-maker's real concern, find evidence that speaks to it, and ask for a small pilot.
AEI.career_lens: Some creative planning jobs continue after approval, through securing a budget and owning adoption. Data may only come back after launch. Ask whether you choose the direction and can investigate and revise it if it doesn't work as expected.
AEI.question: After the last creative proposal was approved for a trial, could a newcomer see the data and revise it again?
AEI.trial: Write two openings for a promotion. Ask someone to choose one and explain any concerns. Ask for a small trial and use their feedback to identify one change you can test.
AEI.decision: If you want to revise creative work around budget and feedback, keep jobs where you can keep improving it. If coordinating adoption was more appealing, also look at project delivery.
AEI.screen: Find out whether a creative role sets the direction, secures resources, and checks what happens after launch.
AEI.hero_job_tip: Find out whether the main work is creating and presenting an idea, securing support, or doing the research that supports the proposal.

EIA.headline: Find what would persuade decision-makers to run a trial
EIA.scene: When a project has gone weeks without a decision, you might want to find out who still has reservations and how to move it forward. Identify the objections, gather enough evidence to answer them, and make the costs of the options easy to compare.
EIA.career_lens: When a role starts by securing a decision, ask what the decision depends on. You might verify evidence and rework the proposal, or take an agreed plan forward. Find out whether you deliver agreement or recommendations.
EIA.question: When a decision-maker asks for important figures, can a newcomer check them and revise the proposal or only coordinate with the people responsible?
EIA.trial: Simulate asking for a trial of two proposals. Discuss the other person's conditions, find one public source, and summarize it in a comparison chart.
EIA.decision: If getting a specific commitment appealed most, keep roles that own the decision process. If research or presentation mattered more, check whether those are regular duties.
EIA.screen: Look for responsibilities that get decisions made. Check whether you can verify the evidence and choose how to present the proposal.
EIA.hero_job_tip: Ask how often you would take part in negotiations and decisions and who provides the evidence and presentation materials.

EAI.headline: Get enough agreement to test a disputed proposal
EAI.scene: You might want to talk with several decision-makers and give each a picture or story that makes the new proposal clear. When someone raises an important doubt, test it with a small sample and see how much the proposal holds up.
EAI.career_lens: Some business planning roles propose partnerships and refine the pitch with a creative team. Others present a completed proposal. Ask who checks feasibility before acceptance and whether you help revise the material.
EAI.question: In the last conversation, could a newcomer change how a partnership was pitched and arrange checks of costs or limits?
EAI.trial: Set two terms for an imaginary partnership and make a one-page pitch. Check one condition that could make it impossible to carry out.
EAI.decision: If you want to keep following through with partners, look for jobs that regularly negotiate terms. If you would rather develop proposals, look for time to produce them.
EAI.screen: Determine whether a partnership role asks for pilots, helps create proposals, or mainly passes them on. Mark who checks feasibility.
EAI.hero_job_tip: In project or business roles, compare time spent creating proposals, securing resources, and testing assumptions.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make evidence clear and traceable
desktop_reading_v1.scene: Two reports disagree about the numbers. Check their definitions against the original records, then build a chart that shows where each figure came from.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare checking figures, presenting information, and managing documents. Identify which activity you would actually do most often.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When the definition used in a report changes, who updates its charts and version notes?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Check one figure against two public sources. Make a chart and record where the number came from and how it was defined.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want to trace the figures and explain them clearly, look for jobs with both access to original tables and control over the final output.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Data analysis and information design both organize information. Analysis often checks how the data were defined, while information design usually has more say in how it is presented. Archiving and versioning can also take a substantial share of the job.

IAC.headline: Explain a discrepancy so others can understand it
IAC.scene: You might ask why two sets of records differ so much under the same rule. Plot the discrepancies so the relationships are visible, then check both sets against the same definitions. That keeps different recording practices from masquerading as a real cause.
IAC.career_lens: If a job emphasizes data and presentation, ask whether you investigate anomalies. Find out whether you deliver a visual analysis or also organize sources, data definitions, and versions so other people can verify it.
IAC.question: When two charts lead to different conclusions, can a newcomer check the original data, change the charts, and leave a traceable record?
IAC.trial: Make a comparison chart using two public data sets. Check what they include and write the dates and reasons for changes alongside the figures.
IAC.decision: If tracing the difference appealed most, keep roles with access to source material. If you enjoyed explaining results or maintaining definitions more, check how much time those tasks get.
IAC.screen: Mark jobs that investigate how figures are defined. Check whether you present the results and own sources and versions.
IAC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can frame new analytical questions, choose how you present the results, and access the original records.

ICA.headline: Find the real problem by checking how the data were defined
ICA.scene: You might want to know why two teams report different figures. Trace the definitions and versions back to the original records, then use a comparison chart to make the findings reusable.
ICA.career_lens: In data quality and reporting roles, distinguish producing figures to a standard from investigating why two sources disagree. Ask whether you can decide how to explain and chart the findings after checking the evidence.
ICA.question: When there are two definitions for one metric, can a newcomer check the sources and propose a common one? Who charts the result?
ICA.trial: Create a fictional spreadsheet with conflicting definitions, find the cause, and write a shared rule with a comparison chart.
ICA.decision: If you want to find further anomalies, look for substantial investigative work. If writing rules or explaining outcomes appealed more, check who owns those outputs.
ICA.screen: Check whether the job includes investigating anomalies, standardizing how they are recorded, and explaining the findings to the people using the data.
ICA.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you can check how data were defined and investigate causes, and how much freedom you have to present findings.

AIC.headline: Turn hard-to-read figures into a chart that shows what's wrong
AIC.scene: You might first try different charts or sequences. Check which makes the real differences easiest to spot. Record the rules for units and labels so the same comparison can be made in the next report.
AIC.career_lens: Some editing and information design roles ask you to make scattered material coherent. Others compile approved drafts. If you want to verify claims too, look for access to primary material, a way to resolve conflicts, and responsibility for the finished version.
AIC.question: When source materials last disagreed, could a newcomer check them again, rewrite the draft, and record the new version?
AIC.trial: Make an information card from two public sources. Verify one apparent conflict and record what you changed, why, and which sources you used.
AIC.decision: If you want to try another way to explain it and verify facts, look at editing or information design. If checking facts and maintaining versions were the draw, compare roles that focus on those tasks.
AIC.screen: Find roles creating original content or layouts. Check whether you also verify facts and keep a version history.
AIC.hero_job_tip: Ask how much you can shape the story in a data-driven content role and whether you can verify the original evidence.

ACI.headline: Set clear rules for how information should be presented
ACI.scene: You might enjoy deciding how a set of reports should look. Set colors, labels, and chart formats, then test the rules with real material and see whether any of them makes crucial information harder to read.
ACI.career_lens: A design system or content standards job can involve inventing a format or keeping existing work consistent. Ask what happens when readers struggle: do you revise the piece within the current rules, or investigate the difficulty and change the rule?
ACI.question: When an existing template leads readers to the wrong conclusion, can a newcomer look at examples and design another template?
ACI.trial: Draw a reference card and give it a reusable format. Find a place where someone could still misunderstand it, then revise it and record why.
ACI.decision: If you want control over the presentation, prioritize design roles. If you most wanted to improve the rules or find causes, check how much time those tasks get.
ACI.screen: Compare time spent choosing layouts, maintaining standards, and investigating where readers struggle. Check who can change the rules.
ACI.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you set standards and revise templates or mainly produce work using templates others have set.

CIA.headline: Make important records easy for a second person to verify
CIA.scene: You might notice that the same metric means different things in different spreadsheets. Check which definitions differ, then make a side-by-side chart showing how to record it consistently for the people who use the figures next.
CIA.career_lens: A documentation standards job helps people find and use the right version. If you also want to investigate, ask who checks original records when definitions conflict and whether you rewrite or illustrate the revised standard.
CIA.question: When a rule leads to recurring errors, can a newcomer check samples to find the cause and update the instructions?
CIA.trial: Sort a fictional register and find two inconsistent categories. Set one rule and use a picture to show how it works.
CIA.decision: If you want to maintain rules and versions, keep process or documentation jobs. If you want to find causes, ask whether the role goes beyond checking records.
CIA.screen: Mark standards maintenance and data review. Ask whether investigating anomalies and making visual instructions are key deliverables.
CIA.hero_job_tip: Find out whether the main work is setting definitions, identifying anomalies, or explaining standards so others can use them.

CAI.headline: Make a reporting standard people can keep following
CAI.scene: You might want to put reporting schedules, input formats, and checks into one clear standard. Use a readable layout to flag exceptions and compare two handovers to see whether it actually prevents omissions.
CAI.career_lens: Information management jobs sometimes turn classification rules into navigation people can understand. Find out whether you can design the rules and the interface prompts. Ask whether they checked lookup time or error records when they last changed a standard.
CAI.question: When categories are updated, does the person maintaining them check entry errors or lookup records? Who sets the format of the guide?
CAI.trial: Sort five fictional records and make an index. Ask someone to find one and note the route they took and where they guessed wrong.
CAI.decision: If consistency was the main attraction, start with maintaining standards. If navigation design or testing appealed more, compare information design and quality analysis.
CAI.screen: Look for jobs where you maintain how information is organized. Check whether you create guides and see whether changes reduce mistakes.
CAI.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the role mainly maintains existing standards or also designs how information is presented and tests any changes.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Understand the problem and get support to change it
desktop_reading_v1.scene: Learners rate training highly and still struggle to use it. Talk to several of them, find where they get stuck, and ask a manager to approve a trial of revised exercises.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare whether the job centers on user research, direct support, or getting the team to implement improvements.
desktop_reading_v1.question: The last time several people got stuck at the same step, who investigated why, changed the approach, and secured a trial?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Pick a common beginner problem. Write two interview questions, two possible causes, and one proposal for a trial.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: Decide which activity you most want to keep doing: investigating the cause, supporting people as things improve, or getting a change officially adopted.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Look separately at interviewing, supporting people over time, and getting a project adopted. Ask whether you follow up on what you hear and whether you are responsible for getting resources when people disagree.

ISE.headline: Investigate a recurring problem on the front line until there's something to fix
ISE.scene: You might want to know why people still make the same mistake after training. Watch them use the tool, ask what they understood, and bring the cause you find to someone who can approve a change.
ISE.career_lens: Research can end at reporting common issues or continue through explaining them to users and asking a team to try a change. Check whether you can interview people and analyze results, then take those results into a pilot.
ISE.question: After a recurring issue was identified, could a newcomer contact people again and try to get one change tested?
ISE.trial: Read three public comments about a service. List possible causes, prepare two interview questions, and propose one change worth testing.
ISE.decision: If you want to understand common difficulties, keep jobs that own investigation. If you want to provide support or secure resources, check who follows through on those tasks.
ISE.screen: In service research, look for investigating repeated problems. Find out whether you can speak to service users and ask for a pilot.
ISE.hero_job_tip: Start with jobs that investigate causes. Ask whether you can meet users and help the changes get adopted.

IES.headline: Use evidence to change how a service works
IES.scene: You might ask why online service requests are repeatedly transferred at a certain time. Check logs and hear what happened from the people involved. Use the evidence to agree on a pilot and help affected users through the change.
IES.career_lens: After analysts on an improvement project report their findings, ask who finds resources and arranges a small trial. If you want to help directly, check whether you answer participants' questions and collect feedback or mainly work with the sponsor.
IES.question: When analysis identifies the main barrier, who negotiates changes and who listens to pilot feedback from participants?
IES.trial: Use fictional activity dropout records to find one cause you can check. Ask someone to agree to a change, then have them try the new process and tell you what happened.
IES.decision: If you most want to gather evidence, prioritize research. If testing adoption and following up was more interesting, check for authority to implement and access to the site.
IES.screen: Find out whether you investigate causes, request resources, and answer questions from participants yourself.
IES.hero_job_tip: Ask whether analysts can initiate a pilot and how much of the role involves working directly with the people who use the service.

SIE.headline: Hear what's hard for people and get a team to respond
SIE.scene: You might care about whether people asking for help actually get it. Hear out each person's situation, look for a barrier they share, and bring examples to the person who could change the process.
SIE.career_lens: In frontline services, a problem that comes up repeatedly is worth asking about. Find out whether you can help the people involved, investigate why it recurs, and use what you find to get the service changed.
SIE.question: After helping someone, can a newcomer review similar cases and recommend changing how the service works?
SIE.trial: Ask someone to show a difficulty finding public information. Help them finish, check one possible shared cause, and write it to the person who could make the change.
SIE.decision: If you want to keep helping people directly, prioritize support. If investigating or getting a change adopted appealed more, look for time to research and a way to propose improvements.
SIE.screen: Compare time spent helping people directly and investigating shared problems. Ask whether the role can use findings to improve the service.
SIE.hero_job_tip: Look for work that helps people directly and gives you time to investigate recurring problems.

SEI.headline: Help someone solve a problem and secure the resources they need
SEI.scene: When several people are waiting for the same support, you may want to respond to the person in front of you first. Get the relevant teams to commit resources, then check whether the delay started in scheduling or case referrals.
SEI.career_lens: When a posting mentions both supporting people and driving progress, ask whether you meet those who need help and can arrange resources. Check whether you finish when the event ends or follow up to see whether the problem was resolved.
SEI.question: After moving resources at short notice, how did a newcomer check whether the people who needed help actually received it?
SEI.trial: Ask someone to simulate two needs. Agree on help you can offer and test it once, then note any problem that remains.
SEI.decision: If you want regular contact with people, keep direct service roles. If coordination or checking the result was the most appealing part, reorder your choices by actual time spent.
SEI.screen: Find direct service work and check whether you can coordinate staff and follow up to see whether the problem got easier.
SEI.hero_job_tip: Ask whether a support role mainly handles individual cases or also coordinates across departments and checks how changes work.

EIS.headline: Move a service change forward and verify the case for it
EIS.scene: You might be drawn to getting two teams to agree to run a service differently. Compare waiting records with feedback, decide which people to include in a trial, and arrange support for them during the change.
EIS.career_lens: Some project roles are judged on who attends or agrees. Others first investigate what support is needed, then explain the change to users and follow up. Ask what informed the last change and who handled feedback on site.
EIS.question: When a project missed its goal, could a newcomer check the records, change the arrangements, and explain them to participants?
EIS.trial: Request a trial for an imaginary event. Set a goal, investigate one obstacle in simulated feedback, and write instructions a participant could use.
EIS.decision: If getting a project past a decision appealed most, look for roles with authority to move it forward. If you preferred investigating or helping directly, check the time allocated to those duties.
EIS.screen: Check whether the job sets goals, investigates obstacles, explains changes to participants, and follows up on results.
EIS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the job involves securing decisions, verifying how changes work, and helping arrange support for users.

ESI.headline: Turn commitments from several groups into help users can receive
ESI.scene: You might want to get a department to set a recurring time for new colleagues to ask questions. Talk to people who need help to see what they are missing, then gather a few weeks of usage to decide whether to keep it.
ESI.career_lens: In recruitment or event organization, ask whether the result is signing people up or making sure they get the support they need. If you also want to investigate, ask whether you can follow up on low participation or why people dropped out.
ESI.question: After sign-up, does this role stay in touch with participants? If turnout is low, who investigates why?
ESI.trial: Simulate recruitment with someone. Agree on the conditions to take part, answer one question, and identify a possible reason for dropping out in a fictional log.
ESI.decision: If you want to keep getting people involved, prioritize coordination. If support or studying participation appealed more, look for roles that own those parts.
ESI.screen: Mark jobs recruiting participants or securing partners. Check whether you also help participants directly and investigate what happens after recruitment.
ESI.hero_job_tip: Find out whether the main deliverable is making resources available or helping users directly, and who evaluates the results.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Turn recurring requests for help into a clear procedure
desktop_reading_v1.scene: Similar problems keep coming back to the help desk. Listen to people who report them, look for patterns in the records, and write searchable guidance that says when to make an exception.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Ask whether the role mainly answers questions using current procedures or can also analyze records and revise the knowledge base.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When the same request keeps coming in, who can examine the tickets and revise the guidance?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Classify three public FAQs, identify one difficulty that keeps coming up, and write a clarification.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If finding patterns and helping people solve problems both appeal to you, consider process improvement roles with access to user feedback.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Education, service, and operations roles can all involve recurring issues. Check whether newcomers mostly answer questions, investigate patterns in the records, or keep the knowledge base and service rules current.

ISC.headline: Trace the cause behind repeated help requests
ISC.scene: You might want to know why people keep making the same mistake when they fill out a form. Listen to one person describe the full sequence and compare similar records. Check whether the instructions, entry point, or rule itself is creating the problem.
ISC.career_lens: You can investigate a service problem by reviewing records or hearing what people found difficult. Ask whether the role lets you use both types of evidence and whether a workable fix makes it into handovers or operating rules.
ISC.question: When the same issue keeps coming up, can a newcomer check records, talk to users, and revise the handover instructions?
ISC.trial: Use three fictional support tickets to identify a shared cause. Ask someone to explain the difficulty and write a handover rule others can check.
ISC.decision: If you want to keep checking the evidence, look for research with access to records and the people involved. If you liked answering questions or maintaining standards, check time in those duties.
ISC.screen: Check whether a job investigates anomalies, hears from people with the problem, and turns findings into service standards.
ISC.hero_job_tip: Start with jobs where you can see individual cases and original records and set analytical questions yourself.

ICS.headline: Turn a vague anomaly into a question you can verify
ICS.scene: Error reports seem to have increased. You might wonder whether more problems are happening or the reporting method has changed. Remove duplicates, use the same categories across the records, and ask a few users where they actually hit an obstacle.
ICS.career_lens: If an analyst also owns data definitions, ask what happens from discovery to closure of an anomaly. Find out whether you can investigate the cause, update the rules, and explain the change to the people who apply it.
ICS.question: When an unusual record appears, does a newcomer return it under the rules, or find the cause, change the rule, and show colleagues how to use it?
ICS.trial: Add a duplicate item to a fictional handover form. Trace why it happened and write a new rule, then ask someone to use it.
ICS.decision: If you want to investigate more discrepancies, look for time to do so. If usable standards appealed more, look for maintaining and teaching the process.
ICS.screen: Mark tasks that trace differences in a process. Check whether you can decide how to record them and explain the rules to the people who apply them.
ICS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the analysis involves checking figures and finding causes or also speaking with the people involved and helping resolve the issue.

SIC.headline: Reach the person who keeps getting stuck
SIC.scene: You might want to hear directly why someone can't finish the process. If several people stop at the same point, compare their circumstances and record what each has already tried so you can follow up.
SIC.career_lens: In support roles, ask whether people keep coming in with similar problems. If you want to go beyond answering on the spot, see whether you can investigate causes, improve handover records, and find out who uses them.
SIC.question: When someone's request can't be resolved on the spot, does a newcomer investigate why and what note do they leave for the next shift?
SIC.trial: Help someone find a document, identify why they got stuck, and leave a note the next person can understand.
SIC.decision: If you want ongoing contact and follow-up, keep direct support. If investigating patterns or clarifying handovers interested you more, look for those tasks in an ordinary week.
SIC.screen: Look for jobs that respond to requests directly. Compare opportunities to investigate common issues and maintain records across shifts.
SIC.hero_job_tip: For support roles, ask whether you can follow up or look for common causes, and how long case notes take.

SCI.headline: Keep support going when somebody else takes over
SCI.scene: Someone has to explain their situation from scratch each time their contact changes. You might pay attention to how to keep support going. Record what's been tried and what comes next, then use follow-up to see which approach works in which cases.
SCI.career_lens: Coaching and service quality can both require tracking progress. If a newcomer gets stuck, ask whether you continue the practice, update their record, or review the records to find why a step is repeatedly missed.
SCI.question: Which errors need another follow-up? Can a coach check earlier records to see why they happened?
SCI.trial: Work through a mock form with someone twice. Note what they repeatedly miss, change one instruction, and see whether it reduces errors.
SCI.decision: If you want to coach and maintain records, look for support roles with follow-up. If the pattern of omissions interested you most, ask about time to analyze it.
SCI.screen: See whether the role involves ongoing coaching or questions. Mark how it records progress and whether you can investigate why people skip the same steps.
SCI.hero_job_tip: Ask how long you support each person and how your time splits between talking, documenting, and finding out why things went wrong.

CIS.headline: Put the records in order so you can explain a service problem
CIS.scene: Service records might appear complete until you discover the same issue filed under different categories. You might want to make them verifiable. When anomalies cluster, work out whether they reflect errors in recording or a real service gap, then find frontline colleagues who can reconnect with affected people.
CIS.career_lens: Intake and review jobs often deal with forms that are returned several times. Ask whether you only check them against the rules or also investigate why they're returned and test clearer instructions with applicants.
CIS.question: If a requirement is commonly misunderstood, can a newcomer measure why forms are returned and explain it to applicants directly?
CIS.trial: Review five fictional applications. Identify one reason for return and write two sentences of guidance for an applicant.
CIS.decision: If you want to keep checking against the rules, look at intake or quality roles. If understanding returns or working with applicants appealed more, find out how much of the job involves those tasks.
CIS.screen: Compare jobs that review applications against standards with those that investigate why items come back and help applicants complete them.
CIS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can change recording standards or investigate exceptions, and whether you also help people directly.

CSI.headline: Make sure every help request is accounted for
CSI.scene: You might notice how often a request was passed on and who still hasn't heard back. Record its status so the next person can follow up, and investigate what's holding up cases that never seem to close.
CSI.career_lens: In process support, ask whether you mainly route requests according to the rules or help people whose situations don't fit them. Find out if you can pull the records to investigate recurring omissions.
CSI.question: When a request is passed on twice and still isn't resolved, does a newcomer investigate, help the applicant, or update the status?
CSI.trial: Set routing rules for fictional requests. Pick one that could go to the wrong team, explain it to someone, and investigate why the error might occur.
CSI.decision: If keeping work traceable was the main appeal, prioritize process duties. To help people or investigate mistakes, find roles with time for that work.
CSI.screen: Find jobs that clearly assign work and maintain records. Check whether you also answer questions and can trace recurring referral errors.
CSI.hero_job_tip: In service process roles, ask whether you mainly follow up on handovers or investigate causes, and whether you deal directly with requests.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Turn evidence into a decision people can act on
desktop_reading_v1.scene: A purchasing proposal is contested. The work can involve checking the costs and risks, securing agreement, and writing down commitments that can be verified at acceptance.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare how much time you get to investigate, what you can negotiate, and your responsibility for implementation.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When a proposal was rejected last time, did you add evidence, renegotiate terms, or change the approval process?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Take a public procurement example. List one question worth checking, one term to negotiate, and one acceptance requirement.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: Put roles involving long-term coordination near the top if you want to track the evidence and also make sure the decision is implemented.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: When a job posting mentions supporting decisions, check whether the daily work involves testing proposals, negotiating commitments, or maintaining the process and reviewing records. Roles differ in how much say they have in the final decision.

IEC.headline: Get someone to own the next step once the problem is clear
IEC.scene: You might ask why purchasing is taking longer. Find the step that is backing up in the records, take the evidence to the people involved, and agree on a measure the team can keep tracking.
IEC.career_lens: In quality improvement or operations analysis, look for work where you can test a problem against evidence. Ask who secures a trial, who sets acceptance checks, and whether you see the results after submitting a recommendation.
IEC.question: After trialing a new approach, can a newcomer verify the data and decide whether to invest further?
IEC.trial: Investigate a delay using simulated data. Propose a small trial, explain what support it needs, and record two acceptance measures.
IEC.decision: If you want to understand the cause and use it to change plans, look for analysis that can follow a pilot. Compare roles in coordination or documentation if those tasks appealed more.
IEC.screen: Find jobs that investigate causes and take findings into a pilot discussion. Check who organizes implementation and who maintains the checks.
IEC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the analysis can change a decision and whether you follow through on implementation and maintain tracking standards.

ICE.headline: Find what's behind a swing in the numbers
ICE.scene: When the numbers drop suddenly, you might want to know what caused it. Compare equivalent batches and check for missing entries. Then bring the verifiable figures to the person who decides what to change first.
ICE.career_lens: In process analysis, check whether you can trace bad records to their source and change the checks as a result. Ask who explains and gets support for the new procedure and what a newcomer would do.
ICE.question: After the last rule change, could a newcomer explain the evidence to another team and coordinate when to switch?
ICE.trial: Find why a fictional handover record doesn't match. Propose a rule and explain to someone how it would reduce mistakes.
ICE.decision: If verifying evidence appealed most, prioritize analysis. If you prefer maintaining or promoting rules, find out what authority those roles have.
ICE.screen: Mark investigating causes and maintaining data definitions. Check whether you also get others to use revised rules.
ICE.hero_job_tip: Find out how much time there is to inspect the original records and whether you can propose and press for a change.

EIC.headline: Use evidence to agree on a goal you can track
EIC.scene: You may be interested in getting several departments to agree on new delivery goals. Compare the figures they bring, establish the cost, and put commitments in a plan with deadlines, owners, and acceptance criteria.
EIC.career_lens: When delivery is late, ask whether you bring the people responsible together, check the evidence for the bottleneck, and add revised commitments to a list of owners. Some roles report the delay and new commitments but hand off any changes.
EIC.question: Who negotiated the revised plan? Can a newcomer inspect evidence for the delay and update who is responsible?
EIC.trial: Imagine two deliveries are late. Agree with someone which comes first. Check a project record and write a new plan others can trace.
EIC.decision: If reaching agreement and following through appealed most, keep coordination roles. If you preferred investigating or documenting what happened, compare time and decision rights in those jobs.
EIC.screen: Find out whether the role renegotiates deadlines or only reports delays. Check whether it investigates bottlenecks and records commitments.
EIC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you provide figures for existing plans or secure resources, get agreement on goals, and verify commitments.

ECI.headline: Record disagreements in a way people can verify
ECI.scene: You might enjoy getting someone to take on work that has no clear owner. After agreeing the schedule, check which promises have been met and investigate stalled items before renegotiating the plan.
ECI.career_lens: In project management, distinguish agreeing on deadlines and responsibilities from maintaining the schedule for others. If milestones keep moving, ask whether you can investigate why and ask for changes.
ECI.question: When milestones repeatedly move, does the role renegotiate deadlines or analyze the record first? Would a newcomer investigate?
ECI.trial: Give a mock project three commitments and verification steps. Add a delay, negotiate another date, and record what might have caused it.
ECI.decision: If you want to own delivery, keep roles that negotiate and track commitments. If finding deviations or keeping records clear was more appealing, look for jobs specializing in that work.
ECI.screen: Compare roles that negotiate commitments, maintain tracking rules, and investigate deviations. Ask how much a coordinator can decide.
ECI.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you mainly negotiate resources and resolve disagreements or maintain a log and track progress.

CIE.headline: Reconcile a set of disputed accounts
CIE.scene: The same project's costs differ sharply between two tables. You might want to trace each entry to its source and check its category. Once the cause is clear, you can discuss what to do with the budget owner using the same figures.
CIE.career_lens: A process role may deliver records others can verify and standards for handling exceptions. If you want to investigate deviations and improve the rules, ask who proposes a change after several exceptions and who gets the team to adopt it.
CIE.question: When a rule repeatedly needs exceptions, can a newcomer check records, draft a revision, and arrange for the relevant people to try it?
CIE.trial: Check five fictional records. Find one justified exception, revise the rule, and ask someone to try it.
CIE.decision: If you want ongoing responsibility for clear rules, look for authority to revise them. If investigation or getting support appealed more, add roles centered on those tasks to your list.
CIE.screen: Find work that maintains rules and investigates anomalies. Ask who approves a revision and who gets the team to adopt it.
CIE.hero_job_tip: Look for work where you can set standards for checking data and investigate differences. Ask whether you help interpret the findings.

CEI.headline: Make commitments, progress, and evidence line up
CEI.scene: It can be hard to tell what each team promised and when it is due. You might want to keep those agreements traceable. When progress stalls, discuss a fix and check the source data if you need to establish what caused the delay.
CEI.career_lens: Compliance operations may involve chasing missing documents or agreeing who owns each record. Ask whether you can sample the evidence when a record is disputed or pass it to a reviewer for judgment.
CEI.question: When a deadline is missed, do you send a reminder, investigate it, or get teams to agree to a different handover rule?
CEI.trial: Make a responsibility table for a mock approval. Check the evidence behind one delay and agree on a revised date with someone.
CEI.decision: If making rules usable and traceable appealed most, keep process jobs. If negotiation or verification was more appealing, compare their share of the work.
CEI.screen: Check whether the job maintains responsibilities and records. Ask whether you also follow up to get work done and verify the evidence.
CEI.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the role mainly sets tracking rules, keeps negotiations moving, or investigates a specific open question.
