desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make an activity that gets people to join in
desktop_reading_v1.scene: Many people sign up for a public class and few keep attending. Try another way to tell the story, observe how learners take part, and ask the team to test the change with the next group.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare creating content, working with learners, and organizing projects using actual tasks from each role.
desktop_reading_v1.question: How did learner feedback change the last course? Who requested extra time or budget to make those changes?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Rewrite the opening of a sign-up page for a subject you know. Then write the first step a reader can take to participate.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If explaining things live was the best part, check how much of the role is teaching. If you would rather develop and run an activity, check what you could decide.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Course design, event operations, and recruiting participants may happen on the same team. Check whether the job mainly designs the experience, works with participants directly, or owns recruitment results.

ASE.headline: Turn a good idea into an experience people can take part in
ASE.scene: How an activity starts can affect whether people stand and watch or get involved. That design choice might interest you. See where participants are still asking for help, then use the plan to request what would make the next session work better.
ASE.career_lens: Some event experience jobs design the activity and see how people take part. Others supply concepts. To follow the design through implementation, check whether you also coordinate the schedule, site, and staffing.
ASE.question: When participants struggled at the last event, could a newcomer change the activity and request help, or only explain it in person?
ASE.trial: Design a short activity and run it with someone. Agree on one kind of support they need and fix one awkward part.
ASE.decision: If you want to design another version, keep creative roles with participant feedback. If coaching or coordinating help appealed more, check the time those duties get.
ASE.screen: Find roles that design activities. Check whether you guide participants directly and can arrange the resources to deliver the design.
ASE.hero_job_tip: Ask how much say you have in designing the experience and whether you also lead participants or contribute to proposals.

AES.headline: Get support for a new way to present an idea
AES.scene: You might want to create an activity people will remember. Present two versions to partners so they can see what each offers, then add guidance for what participants actually need when they arrive.
AES.career_lens: In brand events or content planning, find out whether you decide how to present the idea and are responsible for getting approval. If you also want contact with participants, ask who takes questions and gathers feedback on site.
AES.question: After approval, could a newcomer present the idea, listen to feedback, and revise the design?
AES.trial: Write a card explaining an activity and ask someone to try it. Rewrite the part that caused a question.
AES.decision: If rewriting the explanation appealed most, keep design work. If getting support or answering questions was more engaging, check how often those duties come up.
AES.screen: Mark content decisions you own. Find out who gets approval and who speaks directly with participants.
AES.hero_job_tip: Find out which tasks come up most often: creative production, making a pitch, or helping people on site.

SAE.headline: Help people find a way into the activity
SAE.scene: You may notice someone hanging back because they couldn't follow. Try explaining it a different way and make a visual cue card that helps more people join in. If there aren't enough facilitators, talk through the staffing with the organizer.
SAE.career_lens: First see how much time you spend teaching or supporting people directly. Some teaching and community roles let you arrange materials and coordinate volunteers. Others give you fixed material and ask you to deliver the session.
SAE.question: When participants fell behind last time, could the facilitator revise the materials and arrange extra practice?
SAE.trial: Guide someone through a short exercise. Revise a visual aid where they got stuck, then arrange the next practice session together.
SAE.decision: If you want to keep guiding people, keep roles with regular participant contact. If revising materials or lining up support was the best part, look for jobs with time set aside for it.
SAE.screen: Find jobs that involve guiding or supporting people directly. Then check whether you can adapt their materials and coordinate help.
SAE.hero_job_tip: In teaching or activity roles, ask whether you can help participants directly, adapt materials for them, and arrange extra support.

SEA.headline: Get resources to the people who need help
SEA.scene: You might first listen to what participants want to solve and then arrange space, time, or coaching for them. Redesign the invitation and sign-up so the people who need it can find it.
SEA.career_lens: If you want to work on the front line and be able to arrange resources, ask what you can do when people fall behind. Decide whether you want a role that adds staff or changes guidance or one that mainly responds under existing rules.
SEA.question: If a newcomer can't resolve a request, can they ask a colleague for help and revise the instructions, or only respond with the current process?
SEA.trial: Simulate a request for extra help. Clarify the person's needs, agree on who can assist, and make a follow-up card.
SEA.decision: If you want to keep following a person's needs, keep direct service roles. If arranging help or improving materials was more appealing, compare the jobs that own those tasks.
SEA.screen: Compare jobs that respond to people, arrange help, and write materials. Ask how much the people on the front line can allocate themselves.
SEA.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you work directly with the people receiving support or mostly coordinate partners, and whether you help design service materials.

EAS.headline: Secure what an activity needs to actually go ahead
EAS.scene: You might be most interested in securing support from different groups. Present a distinctive plan so partners can picture the event. Ask participants what they need so you can check what the organizers' commitments will actually make possible.
EAS.career_lens: In event planning or project lead roles, check whether you initiate projects and get the necessary backing. Ask whether you decide how to present the idea and talk to participants to improve the next event.
EAS.question: Once resources are approved, can a newcomer still set the presentation and gather feedback?
EAS.trial: Propose a short activity to someone, agree on conditions, and make a visual invitation. Ask what they would need to know before joining.
EAS.decision: If taking an idea through to people taking part appealed most, look for clear responsibility for getting it started. If creative work or direct service mattered more, check those deliverables.
EAS.screen: Look for jobs that start projects and get support. Find out whether you decide how to present the event and speak directly with participants.
EAS.hero_job_tip: Find out whether most of the role is developing partnerships, creating an event, or facilitating and supporting it afterward.

ESA.headline: Bring different people together to get a service running
ESA.scene: Organizers, volunteers, and the people receiving a service may want different things. Getting them to agree to an arrangement they can carry out might be the part you want most. After hearing what participants need on site, you can also revise outreach and instructions.
ESA.career_lens: In a community or event role, ask whether success means recruiting enough people, running the activity, or responding to their needs over time. If it includes content planning, check who creates the material and who approves it.
ESA.question: From recruitment through the last event, did a newcomer explain the conditions for taking part and revise materials after hearing feedback?
ESA.trial: Ask someone to simulate signing up. Agree on the time and conditions, answer one question, and make the instructions clearer.
ESA.decision: If getting people to take part appeals, prioritize organizational work. If answering questions or revising content mattered most, check how often those tasks come up.
ESA.screen: Look at who organizes participation and owns the result. Compare time answering questions and creating materials.
ESA.hero_job_tip: Ask how results are measured: resources secured, people helped, or activity materials delivered.

positive_value: The value of this content is to break the clues into observable small tasks: Artistic focuses on expression, style, narrative, form, and experience; Social focuses on real people, understanding, support, communication, and collaboration; Conventional focuses on rules, data, processes, order, and reviewable records. Whichever comes first only indicates which activity to gather evidence from first. These clues offer exploration questions, not job answers.

Record only which action you most want to continue.

secondary_support_line: Then consider the second dimension, Social: use it as an additional observation entry point and record whether real people, understanding, support, communication, and collaboration make the task more appealing.
tertiary_stabilizer: The third dimension, Conventional, is only an additional clue: observe whether rules, data, processes, order, and reviewable records help distinguish more specific task conditions.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make materials people can keep using
desktop_reading_v1.scene: Learners regularly get stuck on the same exercise. Try a clearer illustration. Record updates and feedback so the next person can keep improving the material.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Identify which tasks you would regularly do: making materials, coaching people, or maintaining training resources.
desktop_reading_v1.question: After a revision, who looks at how the materials are used and maintains templates, versions, and exceptions?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Pick a public tutorial and present it in a different form. Add the version date and clarify one common misunderstanding.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want creative work and the responsibility to maintain what you make, compare learning resources and knowledge management roles with one-off event work.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Instructional design and training operations both work with course materials. One may try new ways of teaching while the other keeps versions, schedules, and feedback records in order. Some roles also coach people in person.

ASC.headline: Make learning materials easy to understand and hand over
ASC.scene: You might want to turn a dry set of instructions into a story or a set of illustrated cards. Try the material with a newcomer, see what they need spelled out, and leave the layout and revision rules for the colleague who takes over.
ASC.career_lens: An education content job that designs exercises, observes learners, and maintains editions spans teaching and operations. Ask whether you choose how to teach the material and how much time goes to maintaining versions.
ASC.question: After trying a lesson, can a newcomer revise an example and update the course version?
ASC.trial: Make a one-page exercise for a familiar skill. Try it with someone, change a prompt, and record the new version.
ASC.decision: If you want to keep trying ways to explain something, look at instructional design. If coaching people or maintaining material appealed more, compare those duties by time.
ASC.screen: Find jobs that design teaching material and observe people using it. Check whether you also keep editions current.
ASC.hero_job_tip: Ask who decides how materials are presented, who pilots them, and who keeps track of versions after release.

ACS.headline: Make the same materials useful in different settings
ACS.scene: Schools, shops, and internal trainers use the same material. You might enjoy making it consistent and still leaving room to adapt it on site. A template keeps the basic structure while letting instructors choose examples that fit their learners.
ACS.career_lens: For roles that combine presentation and standards, ask who decides layouts and examples and who updates the reference numbers and proofreads. Find out whether you train colleagues when a new template is introduced.
ACS.question: After releasing a template, does the designer show colleagues how to use it and update rules for exceptions?
ACS.trial: Draw two illustrated cards with a shared layout rule. Show someone how to use one and ask what questions they have.
ACS.decision: If you want to create new formats, check design authority. If you also want to keep standards current or show others how to use them, check who owns those tasks.
ACS.screen: Look for work that sets layouts and standards and teaches people how to use them. Check whether all three are in one role.
ACS.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you set presentation standards or apply templates and whether you can revise materials with the people who use them.

SAC.headline: Help someone learn and build practice that suits them
SAC.scene: Someone can understand a rule and still need practice to carry it out. You might want to work alongside them until they can do a step independently. Use examples that connect to their experience and note the progress and feedback so the next session can pick up there.
SAC.career_lens: If you can adapt your coaching to learners' progress, find out whether you update the course materials with the revised diagrams. One-to-one coaching and maintaining shared materials are separate responsibilities.
SAC.question: When learners have the same trouble repeatedly, can the coach revise the materials and let the next group try the new version?
SAC.trial: Teach someone a small, safe task, rewrite one instruction they misunderstood, and mark the new version for the next session.
SAC.decision: If helping people work independently is most appealing, keep practical coaching. If revising guides or maintaining material drew you in, check which duties you would repeat.
SAC.screen: Mark jobs that coach people, rewrite instructions, and maintain training material. Check whether you can continue working with the same learners.
SAC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can coach participants, design your own exercises, and how closely you have to track progress.

SCA.headline: Give each learner a way to keep going
SCA.scene: You might care most about keeping someone's learning on track when their instructor changes. Record where each person got to so the next teacher can choose another material or explanation to get them past the difficult part.
SCA.career_lens: Support jobs need records. Some end when you close the ticket. Others require updating handover rules in response to recurring requests. If you want to try different ways of explaining things, ask whether you can revise the guidance and see how people use it.
SCA.question: If frontline staff see people misreading a guide, can a newcomer rewrite it and record the change?
SCA.trial: Help someone with a common question, note the solution and when to hand it over, then make a visual reminder.
SCA.decision: If you want to keep answering questions, keep direct support. If improving processes or making prompts was most appealing, look for roles that deliver those outcomes.
SCA.screen: Look for work with users. Ask who maintains handover rules and help prompts, including whether frontline staff can change them.
SCA.hero_job_tip: Look for ongoing learner support. Find out who maintains progress records and whether you can tailor materials to individuals.

CAS.headline: Keep track of the versions and uses of training material
CAS.scene: Several guides claim to be current, leaving the next person unsure which to trust. You might want to sort out versions and update rules, then make a clear index that tells users where to start.
CAS.career_lens: In course or materials operations, first ask whether the focus is getting everyone the right version. If you want to improve the content and help people use it, ask whether you can redesign materials and explain them directly alongside publishing and updating files.
CAS.question: When colleagues don't know which version to use, does the role trace the source and publish the right one, or also demonstrate it?
CAS.trial: Arrange the release order of two mock course versions. Make a guide card and ask someone to use it to find the right version.
CAS.decision: If keeping the versions consistent appealed most, look at content operations. If presenting a guide or helping users interested you more, check whether those duties get regular time.
CAS.screen: Find out who manages versions and release. Check whether the role also designs explanations and shows users how to apply them.
CAS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you set content standards and whether you can also design materials and help the people who use them.

CSA.headline: Keep practical support going through a handover
CSA.scene: For support to continue, the next person needs to know what someone has practiced and where they still need help. You might want to organize those records and turn common questions into a one-page visual guide for the colleague taking over.
CSA.career_lens: A records service can file information so it's easy to find or help people directly locate what they need. Ask whether you can change the navigation or revise the material when users keep looking in the wrong place.
CSA.question: If materials are filed correctly but users keep going to the wrong place, will their maintainer ask them about it and revise the entry point?
CSA.trial: Organize five fictional documents. Help someone find one, then change a category name and an instruction where they got stuck.
CSA.decision: If keeping materials easy to find appealed, look at information management. If helping people find them or revising them was more engaging, check access to users and control over editing.
CSA.screen: Mark how materials are categorized and how issues are followed up. Check whether you can talk to users and revise content.
CSA.hero_job_tip: Distinguish maintaining records from following up one-on-one and creating explanations.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Deliver a creative idea within real constraints
desktop_reading_v1.scene: An event proposal looks good and still has to fit a budget, distribution format, and launch date. Adapt how it is presented, make the case for what should take priority, and record the version and acceptance requirements.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Identify whether the role develops creative work, secures resources, or manages delivery, and who decides how much can change.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When a piece needed a last-minute revision, who decided the final version and organized help to get it out?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Write two headlines for the same event poster and make a checklist for publishing it.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If developing the message matters most, look for roles where you can make creative choices. If you also want to coordinate delivery, compare content project roles.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Content projects and marketing operations both coordinate schedules. Check whether the job lets you make creative decisions or mostly tracks budgets, schedules, and publishing requirements.

AEC.headline: Deliver a distinctive idea on time
AEC.scene: You might most want to set an event's style and how it is presented. Use sketches to agree on a clear scope, then set specifications, reviews, and version milestones so later revisions stay on track.
AEC.career_lens: In creative delivery, check whether you decide the proposal. If you also coordinate budget and adoption after approval, find out who documents specifications and versions and whether you own delivery as well as the creative work.
AEC.question: After a creative idea is approved, does a newcomer follow budget and specifications? Which parts can they set themselves?
AEC.trial: Make a one-page proposal for an imaginary project. Ask someone to agree to a trial and list the specifications the next person must retain.
AEC.decision: If you want to try different versions, look for creative decision-making. If getting agreement or maintaining consistent specifications appealed most, compare those responsibilities separately.
AEC.screen: Find jobs that make creative decisions, then check who gets approval and what standards the work must meet at handover.
AEC.hero_job_tip: Ask how many creative decisions you own and whether you would pitch the work and manage scope and versions.

ACE.headline: Set workable rules for producing a series of pieces
ACE.scene: A set of designs needs to look good and still make sense when new pieces appear next month. You might enjoy setting a style for the series. Once you have a shared template and update rules, explain to each client which requirements can vary.
ACE.career_lens: To turn design work into shared standards, ask who decides layouts, rules, and exceptions. Find out whether you encourage other teams to use them and whether difficulties in adoption can lead to design changes.
ACE.question: If a template conflicts with a department's current process, who can change the standard and agree on a switch?
ACE.trial: Make two information cards for the same subject. Set a shared rule, ask someone to try it, and record one part of the rule to revise.
ACE.decision: If you want to work on creative decisions and standards together, keep design systems roles. If adoption work appealed most, ask whether it is a core duty.
ACE.screen: Look for roles with decisions about how work is presented and the standards it follows. Find out whether you get other teams to adopt them.
ACE.hero_job_tip: Look for jobs where you can set design standards. Ask whether client conversations are occasional or a core duty.

EAC.headline: Agree on a creative project with clear boundaries
EAC.scene: You might enjoy turning a client's vague expectations into choices both sides can confirm. Use two sketches to clarify what matters, then document the scope, versions, and acceptance criteria so the team can work from them.
EAC.career_lens: If a role is responsible for winning a proposal, find out whether you can decide how to present it with the team. Once the commitment is made, ask whether you also track schedules, versions, and acceptance. That will change where you spend most of your time.
EAC.question: Once a project goes ahead, does a newcomer track versions, progress, and sign-off? Can they help decide how to present the proposal?
EAC.trial: Simulate asking for a trial. Make a one-page proposal, agree on a delivery, and record three commitments someone can check.
EAC.decision: If getting an agreement and delivering on it appealed most, look at project roles. If you preferred design or tracking delivery, compare the time spent on those tasks.
EAC.screen: Compare getting a proposal approved, shaping how it looks, and tracking what gets delivered. First identify the commitment the role owns.
EAC.hero_job_tip: Find out whether your primary deliverable is securing projects, creating the concept, or managing scope and deadlines.

ECA.headline: Find a way forward that several groups can support
ECA.scene: Every group asks for a change and nobody can make the final call. You might want to help them choose a feasible direction. Put the budget and approval steps on a schedule so people can compare the creative options against the same limits.
ECA.career_lens: Coordination roles can deliver agreed staffing and budgets or records showing each milestone is complete. If you want to help communicate changes, find out whether you create those messages or distribute notices someone else prepares.
ECA.question: In the last change across teams, did a newcomer prepare handover materials? Which rules could they set?
ECA.trial: Simulate a schedule change with someone. Agree on priorities, make a handover table, and diagram which teams or tasks the change affects.
ECA.decision: If coordinating changes and following through on commitments appealed most, keep project coordination roles. If standards or communication mattered more, explore roles centered on those duties.
ECA.screen: Look for roles that arrange resources and set handover rules. Ask whether the coordinator creates the material communicating a change.
ECA.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you mainly bring people on board and coordinate them, or also own the process and help make creative decisions.

CAE.headline: Make design handover rules clear and usable
CAE.scene: You might pay attention to keeping old drafts out of circulation after a revision. Set rules for naming and checking files, show how they apply to different designs, and make the case for partners to use the same approach.
CAE.career_lens: Check whether a job applies standards or develops standards others can use repeatedly. The latter can include illustrating the rules, answering teams' questions, and getting everyone to adopt one approach.
CAE.question: If two teams enter different information in the same field, can a newcomer revise the rule, make examples, and organize a trial?
CAE.trial: Set a shared rule for five records, draw a comparison, and agree to test it with someone. Record one exception.
CAE.decision: If you want to keep maintaining standards, prioritize that responsibility. If explaining or promoting them appealed more, check whether it gets enough time.
CAE.screen: Prioritize roles that write and maintain standards. Check whether you can present them in an understandable form and help people adopt them.
CAE.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can change the rules and the presentation, and how much of the role involves getting people to adopt them.

CEA.headline: Turn project agreements into a process people can follow
CEA.scene: You might enjoy turning informal comments into traceable requirements. Agree on who approves what, then diagram a round of revisions so a new teammate can tell where the work stands.
CEA.career_lens: When teams keep using old procedures during a transition, ask who tracks exceptions and negotiates the switch date. Find out whether you can rewrite notices or diagrams to help the people who take over.
CEA.question: When an old process is still in use, can a newcomer track exceptions, agree on a switch date, and revise the guide?
CEA.trial: Make a transition and exceptions table for a fictional process. Agree on a date and draw how the old steps map to the new ones.
CEA.decision: If you want to make the transition traceable, look at process management. If coordination or presentation appealed more, check the mix of duties.
CEA.screen: Start with maintaining a process. Find out who coordinates the switch to a new one and who communicates changes to the people doing the work.
CEA.hero_job_tip: Find out whether the daily work mainly tracks progress, coordinates the people responsible, or creates the materials needed to deliver.

desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make support for people consistent and reliable
desktop_reading_v1.scene: People seeking help keep being passed from one team to another. Listen to what they're dealing with, agree on who is responsible, and establish when to follow up and who handles exceptions.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare time spent helping, coordinating, and keeping records. Ask whether the role can change how cases are referred.
desktop_reading_v1.question: When a cross-team request was not resolved in time, who could reassign the work?
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Map a public service procedure. Show where a person asks for help, who takes it, and where exceptions go.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If working directly with users appeals to you, check how much time the role gives you with them. If you like coordinating, clarify what decisions you can make.
desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Service and operations roles both involve talking to people. Check whether most of the time goes to supporting people directly, coordinating teams, or checking that handovers follow the agreed procedure.

SEC.headline: Remove an unnecessary step for someone seeking help
SEC.scene: Someone has waited several days for help. You might want to hear what they need to resolve first, contact the team that can help, and leave the next steps and contact details together in one record.
SEC.career_lens: In service coordination, ask whether you deal directly with people who need help and whether you can arrange resources. Find out whether you finish when coverage is scheduled or track the outcome and prepare the next shift to follow up.
SEC.question: When the last request couldn't be resolved on the spot, whom could a newcomer contact and what did they hand over?
SEC.trial: Simulate a help request. Clarify the difficulty, agree with someone who does what, and leave three handover notes.
SEC.decision: If you want to keep checking in with the person, prioritize direct support. If organizing help or keeping clear records was more engaging, look for those duties.
SEC.screen: Check time spent helping people directly. Find out whether you can arrange resources and leave a record for the next shift.
SEC.hero_job_tip: Start with roles that serve people directly. Ask whether you can help secure resources and see what happens once people receive them.

SCE.headline: Make sure every request for help gets followed up
SCE.scene: You might want to listen long enough to understand what happened and spare the person from repeating their story. Keep a clear record of the case, then find the right person to help when a request exceeds your authority.
SCE.career_lens: In intake or support roles, ask whether you resolve problems yourself or mostly record and refer them. If similar issues recur, ask whether you can bring the people responsible together to change how cases are handed over.
SCE.question: When a problem keeps recurring, can a newcomer change the handover practice and ask the right group to try it?
SCE.trial: Help someone complete a mock repair request. Note what the next shift needs and discuss a change to one rule that repeatedly causes errors.
SCE.decision: If you want to keep solving specific problems, look for direct contact with users. If you prefer improving the process, ask whether you can propose and implement changes.
SCE.screen: Compare answering requests, keeping records, and getting changes adopted. Find out what happens after the initial service.
SCE.hero_job_tip: Compare time spent on case support and follow-up records. Ask whether you can reach a decision-maker when a case gets stuck.

ESC.headline: Secure resources to close a service gap
ESC.scene: Several organizations can each offer a little. You might want to negotiate a plan that closes the actual service gap. Confirm the most urgent needs with the people using the service and document what's available, who follows up, and when it will be reviewed.
ESC.career_lens: In community projects or service operations, check what participation and partnership results you own. If you also want to help users directly, ask how much time you have for questions and who maintains the records.
ESC.question: At the start of a project, does a newcomer who arranges staffing also handle questions from users? Who maintains the handover?
ESC.trial: Simulate starting a small activity. Agree on responsibilities, answer a sign-up question, and write a note for the next shift.
ESC.decision: If bringing in people and organizing action appealed most, look for responsibility for implementation. If you would prefer working with users or organizing records, compare roles centered on those tasks.
ESC.screen: Find out whether you initiate and organize work. Check who answers questions directly and who maintains the records over time.
ESC.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you mainly develop partnerships and find resources, and whether you can speak with the people who use the service.

ECS.headline: Agree on resources and responsibilities and get them to the people doing the work
ECS.scene: You might be drawn to getting people to make genuine commitments to a project. Once you agree on staffing, budget, and acceptance criteria, see whether the people you serve can get help under the new setup.
ECS.career_lens: When a project or service role needs to keep teams on schedule, ask whether you set procedures and negotiate responsibilities and delivery. Find out whether you also confirm with users that a process change solved their problem.
ECS.question: After a new arrangement starts, how does a newcomer find out whether frontline teams adopted it and whether users can use it?
ECS.trial: Agree on a change to a service with someone. Write who is responsible, then ask them to try it as a user.
ECS.decision: If you want to follow an agreement through to delivery, look for roles that can set the plan. If you most want to maintain rules or answer requests, compare a typical day in each job.
ECS.screen: Look for work that puts plans into practice across teams. Check whether you set rules and verify that actual users get the help they need.
ECS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you own the outcomes of a partnership and how much time goes to checking delivery and following up with people.

CSE.headline: Keep the handover organized so nobody asking for help is left waiting
CSE.scene: When someone new takes over the shift, can they make sense of the help request? You might want to organize the record so they can pick up where you stopped. Check with the person what remains unresolved and involve another team if needed.
CSE.career_lens: For an intake role, ask what happened with a recent exceptional request. Did the role check documents, help the applicant complete them, or also negotiate a change with another team?
CSE.question: When none of the standard options fits an application, can a newcomer explain what is missing, record the exception, and ask for a rule change?
CSE.trial: Write intake conditions for three fictional applications. Explain one exception to someone and agree on how to handle a repeat.
CSE.decision: If you want to keep making the rules clear in practice, prioritize intake or process jobs. If helping people or getting a change adopted appealed more, check time for those tasks.
CSE.screen: Find roles that apply intake rules and help applicants directly. Check whether you can also discuss changes with other teams.
CSE.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the focus is keeping records or helping people directly, and whether you help coordinate exceptions.

CES.headline: Set clear, workable rules for making resources available
CES.scene: You might want to manage appointments, places, and responsibilities under the same rules. When the arrangement leaves someone out, find out what changes the relevant teams can agree to and explain how the new arrangement works.
CES.career_lens: If you want to make a process usable, first check whether you can maintain and revise its rules. Then find out whether you secure agreement and organize adoption or also hear directly from users after the change.
CES.question: After a rule changes, who gets groups to use it? Can a newcomer hear directly what still doesn't work for users?
CES.trial: Revise a fictional handover rule. Agree with someone on where to try it, ask them to walk through it, and record an issue.
CES.decision: If you want to keep improving and maintaining rules, look for process responsibilities. If coordinating adoption or hearing feedback appealed more, check how much time those tasks get.
CES.screen: Mark maintaining standards and coordinating adoption. Ask who hears from the people using the rules and checks how the change worked.
CES.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you usually maintain the rules, negotiate exceptions, or help people complete the task directly.
